Taleb shows that an investor with a strong edge might still see losses on a large share of individual days, so checking returns constantly creates emotional pain without useful information. Viewing results over longer periods reveals the signal. He advises consuming less news and data, since frequent updates amplify randomness and lead to poor decisions.

contagious-03.cue: How do triggers keep a product top of mind?
contagious-03.point: A trigger is something in the environment that reminds people of your product. Kit Kat linked itself to coffee breaks, which happen every day, and sales rose. Effective triggers occur often, stay relevant for a long time, appear near where people can buy or talk, are not already owned by another brand and fit your audience's surroundings. Top of mind means tip of tongue.

imagined-communities-02.cue: What role did print capitalism play in creating nations?
imagined-communities-02.point: Anderson argues that the printing press, combined with capitalism's search for markets, created standardized vernacular languages. Books and newspapers in shared languages allowed people across a territory to imagine themselves reading the same news at the same time, forming a shared community. The newspaper especially created a sense of simultaneous experience among strangers. This made national consciousness possible.

how-not-to-die-06.cue: How can you think of daily calories like a budget?
how-not-to-die-06.point: Imagine you have about 2,000 calories to spend each day. An 800-calorie burger uses up the same budget as several sweet potatoes or many cups of broccoli, which deliver far more nutrients and fiber. Plant foods may cost more per calorie than junk food, but Greger notes they deliver far more nutrition per dollar, making them a better investment in your health.

the-happiness-hypothesis-05.cue: Where does happiness come from, according to Haidt?
the-happiness-hypothesis-05.point: Haidt concludes that happiness comes from between: from getting the right relationships between yourself and others, yourself and your work, and yourself and something larger than yourself. Love and attachment, vital engagement in meaningful work, and a sense of connection to a larger purpose produce lasting happiness. It is not found solely within ourselves or in external circumstances.

talk-like-ted-02.also: Made to Stick; The Charisma Myth
talk-like-ted-02.point: First, unleash the master within: passion is contagious, so speak about what you love. Second, master the art of storytelling: personal stories, stories about others and brand stories build connection. Bryan Stevenson's talk used stories for about two thirds of its time. Third, have a conversation: practice relentlessly until the delivery feels natural, using body language, pacing and tone.

the-whole-brain-child-02.cue: What is connect and redirect, and name it to tame it?
the-whole-brain-child-02.point: When a child is upset, the right brain, emotional and nonverbal, dominates. Parents should first connect emotionally, through empathy, touch and tone, before redirecting with logical explanations from the left brain. Name it to tame it means helping children tell the story of upsetting experiences, which helps them make sense of emotions and reduces their intensity. Storytelling integrates both hemispheres.

the-chimp-paradox-04.also: Meditations; The Obstacle Is the Way
the-chimp-paradox-04.cue: What is the Stone of Life?
the-chimp-paradox-04.point: The Stone of Life represents your core values and truths about life, stored in the Computer as a reference point. Peters suggests writing down principles such as "life is not fair," "I am not perfect" and "my values matter," which provide stability during emotional turbulence. When the Chimp reacts, consulting the Stone of Life reminds the Human what truly matters and helps restore perspective.

shoe-dog-01.point: Phil Knight's memoir tells the story of founding Nike, from his crazy idea in 1962 to import Japanese running shoes to the company's 1980 IPO. He started Blue Ribbon Sports with his former track coach Bill Bowerman, selling Onitsuka Tiger shoes from his car. The memoir is candid about the chaos, near bankruptcies and doubts of building a company. Knight wrote it decades later, reflecting on what mattered.

radical-candor-01.cue: What are the two dimensions of Radical Candor?
radical-candor-01.point: Care personally and challenge directly. Kim Scott defines Radical Candor as caring about someone as a whole person while also telling them clearly when their work falls short. Most of us were taught to choose between being nice and being honest. Scott argues that the kindest thing a boss can do is give clear, direct feedback, because it shows you believe the person can improve.

profit-first-02.cue: How does the Profit First account system work?
profit-first-02.point: Michalowicz recommends opening separate bank accounts: Income, Profit, Owner's Pay, Tax and Operating Expenses. All revenue goes into Income, then twice a month, transfer set percentages into each account. The Profit account is kept at a separate bank to make it harder to access. Seeing small balances in Operating Expenses forces owners to cut costs. Quarterly, a portion of profit is distributed to the owner.

skin-in-the-game-03.point: Taleb argues that an intransigent minority can impose its preferences on everyone when the majority is flexible. For example, if a small share of people only eat kosher food, food producers find it easier to make everything kosher, since others don't mind. The same dynamic shapes language, rules and norms. A determined minority with skin in the game can shift society more than a passive majority.

learning-how-to-learn-04.cue: How does sleep help you learn?
learning-how-to-learn-04.point: Active recall starts the growth of new dendritic spines, the tiny connection points on neurons, but they mainly grow while you sleep. Sleep also clears away unused connections, moves new memories from the hippocampus into long-term storage in the cortex and flushes out toxins that build up while you are awake. Studying right before sleep and reviewing the next morning makes learning stick.

make-it-stick-03.cue: How should practice be spaced over time?
make-it-stick-03.point: Cramming one topic gives quick gains that vanish. Spacing practice out gives the brain time to consolidate new knowledge into long-term memory. The most effective schedule starts with a short delay before the first test, then keeps testing at widening intervals, even after you feel you have mastered the material. This is the principle behind spaced repetition apps like the one you are using now.

blue-ocean-strategy-06.cue: How should you price a blue ocean offering?
blue-ocean-strategy-06.point: Start with price, then work back to cost. First identify the price range of the alternatives customers already use, including other industries. Pick a point in that range based on how easy your offering is to copy: the stronger your patents or advantages, the higher you can go, while network effects or economies of scale favor a low price for mass adoption. Then design costs to hit your target profit.

flow-07.cue: What is the paradox of work and leisure?
flow-07.point: In studies where people were paged at random moments, they were in flow 54 percent of the time at work but only 18 percent during leisure, which mostly meant passive activities like TV. Yet people said they wanted to work less and have more free time. Csikszentmihalyi argues we should recognize the flow opportunities in our work and make leisure more active and challenging.

how-to-stop-worrying-and-start-living-01.cue: What is Dale Carnegie's approach to worry?
how-to-stop-worrying-and-start-living-01.point: Carnegie, author of How to Win Friends and Influence People, collected advice from history, philosophy and readers to help people overcome worry. His central advice is to live in day tight compartments: focus on today rather than regretting yesterday or fearing tomorrow. Worry wastes energy and harms health, while focusing on the present lets you act on what you can control. The book was published in 1948.

the-intelligent-investor-01.also: Poor Charlie's Almanack; A Random Walk Down Wall Street
the-intelligent-investor-01.cue: What is the difference between investing and speculating, according to Graham?
the-intelligent-investor-01.point: Benjamin Graham defines an investment operation as one that, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Anything else is speculation. Investors focus on the underlying business value, while speculators bet on price movements. Graham does not forbid speculation but insists people know the difference and limit speculation to a small portion of their capital. Warren Buffett called this the best book about investing ever written.

high-output-management-04.also: The One Minute Manager; Turn the Ship Around!
high-output-management-04.point: Grove argues the best management style depends on an employee's task relevant maturity, their experience and competence for a specific task. For low maturity, managers should give structured, detailed instructions. As maturity increases, managers should shift to more communication and support, and finally to minimal involvement, monitoring results. The same person may need different styles for different tasks.

no-drama-discipline-05.also: The Whole-Brain Child; The Coaching Habit
no-drama-discipline-05.cue: What redirection strategies do the authors suggest?
no-drama-discipline-05.point: Strategies include reducing words, since lectures overwhelm; embracing emotions while setting limits on behavior; describing rather than preaching; involving children in discipline by asking for their ideas; reframing a no as a yes with conditions; emphasizing the positive; and creatively approaching situations, with humor or play. Teaching mindsight, awareness of their own minds, helps children manage themselves.

money-master-the-game-02.also: The Automatic Millionaire; The Richest Man in Babylon
money-master-the-game-02.cue: What is the first and most important step in Robbins's plan?
money-master-the-game-02.point: The first step is to make the most important financial decision of your life: commit to saving a percentage of your income and investing it automatically. Robbins calls this becoming an investor rather than a consumer. He compares it to building a money machine that works while you sleep. Without this habit, no investment strategy will make you wealthy. Saving even small amounts consistently matters because of compounding.

the-goal-03.also: Thinking in Systems; Good Strategy Bad Strategy
the-goal-03.cue: What is a bottleneck and why does it matter?
the-goal-03.point: A bottleneck is any resource whose capacity is less than the demand placed on it. The output of the whole system is limited by its bottleneck, so an hour lost at a bottleneck is an hour lost for the entire system, while an hour saved elsewhere is meaningless. Alex learns this on a scouting hike where the slowest boy, Herbie, determines the pace of the troop.

the-art-of-the-deal-05.cue: How did the Grand Hyatt deal illustrate the book's methods?
the-art-of-the-deal-05.point: Trump describes acquiring the bankrupt Commodore Hotel near Grand Central Station in the 1970s, when New York was in fiscal crisis. He secured an option to buy, a partnership with Hyatt, financing, and a significant tax abatement from the city by presenting the project as vital to the area's revival. He combined these elements simultaneously, using each commitment to win the others. The deal launched his Manhattan career.

good-to-great-06.also: The Compound Effect; Great by Choice
good-to-great-06.cue: What are the flywheel and the doom loop?
good-to-great-06.point: Good to great transformations didn't happen in one dramatic moment. They resulted from consistent effort in a clear direction, like pushing a heavy flywheel that slowly builds momentum. Comparison companies fell into the doom loop: launching new programs, chasing fads, making acquisitions and changing direction, never building momentum. A culture of discipline and technology accelerators support the flywheel.

the-happiness-trap-04.also: Man's Search for Meaning; The Courage to Be Disliked
the-happiness-trap-04.cue: What role do values play in ACT?
the-happiness-trap-04.point: Harris defines values as how you want to behave as a human being, what you want to stand for. Unlike goals, values are never completed; they guide ongoing action. ACT encourages people to identify their values in areas like relationships, work and health, and take committed action toward them, even when uncomfortable. Living by values creates a rich, meaningful life, even with pain.

the-one-thing-01.point: Gary Keller, cofounder of Keller Williams Realty, and Jay Papasan argue that extraordinary results come from narrowing your focus to the one most important thing. They pose the Focusing Question: "What's the ONE Thing I can do such that by doing it everything else will be easier or unnecessary?" Asking this repeatedly, for life, the year and the day, helps cut through distractions and find leverage.

so-good-they-can-t-ignore-you-07.cue: What is the law of financial viability, or law of payment?
so-good-they-can-t-ignore-you-07.point: A test borrowed from entrepreneur Derek Sivers for deciding when to make a bold move toward autonomy: do it only if people are willing to pay you for it. Payment can mean customers, a job offer, a loan or investors. Sivers became a full-time musician only once music earned more than his day job. Money is a neutral signal of whether your skills are valuable enough yet.

extreme-ownership-03.also: Team of Teams; The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
extreme-ownership-03.point: Cover and move is the basic military tactic where one team provides protective fire while another moves, then they switch. The broader principle is that teams within an organization must support each other rather than compete or blame. Departments should work together toward the overall mission. Willink describes how units that ignored this caused friendly fire and failure.

capitalism-and-freedom-05.cue: What is the negative income tax?
capitalism-and-freedom-05.point: Friedman proposed replacing the patchwork of welfare programs with a negative income tax. People earning below a threshold would receive a payment from the government, scaled so that earning more always leaves them better off. He argued it would help the poor directly, reduce bureaucracy, and preserve incentives to work. The idea influenced the Earned Income Tax Credit in the United States and later debates about universal basic income.

the-lessons-of-history-01.cue: What is The Lessons of History?
the-lessons-of-history-01.point: After completing their eleven volume Story of Civilization, Will and Ariel Durant wrote this short book in 1968 summarizing what history teaches about human nature, government, religion, war and economics. They approach history skeptically, noting most of it is guessing and the rest prejudice, yet they draw lessons from patterns across civilizations. The book is brief, about a hundred pages, and filled with memorable observations.

leadership-and-self-deception-04.also: Daring Greatly; The Art of Loving
leadership-and-self-deception-04.cue: How do we get out of the box?
leadership-and-self-deception-04.point: The authors argue that techniques like communication skills don't work if we remain in the box, since people sense our attitude. We get out by seeing others as people with their own needs and concerns, and by questioning our own virtue. Once we stop resisting what we sense we should do for others, we are out of the box. Leaders must focus on results while honoring the humanity of others.

the-hacker-s-diet-02.cue: Why does Walker recommend a moving average of weight?
the-hacker-s-diet-02.point: Daily weight fluctuates by several pounds because of water, food and other factors, which can be misleading and discouraging. Walker recommends weighing yourself every day and plotting a moving average, which smooths out noise and reveals the true trend. This trend line shows whether you are losing, gaining or maintaining. It also lets you calculate your actual daily calorie deficit from the data.

the-happiness-advantage-02.also: The Gifts of Imperfection; The Happiness Project
the-happiness-advantage-02.point: After playing Tetris for hours, people start seeing shapes fitting together everywhere. Achor uses this to describe how our brains get stuck in patterns. People who focus on problems start seeing problems everywhere. By training the brain to scan for positives, such as writing down three good things each day, we can develop a positive Tetris effect that helps us notice opportunities.

the-22-immutable-laws-of-marketing-03.cue: What are the Law of the Mind and the Law of Focus?
the-22-immutable-laws-of-marketing-03.point: The Law of the Mind says it is better to be first in the prospect's mind than first in the marketplace. The Law of Focus says the most powerful concept in marketing is owning a word in the prospect's mind. Volvo owns safety, and FedEx owned overnight. A company should choose a simple, benefit oriented word and sacrifice other attributes to keep that focus.

the-structure-of-scientific-revolutions-.also: The Black Swan; Black Box Thinking
the-structure-of-scientific-revolutions-.cue: How do anomalies lead to crisis?
the-structure-of-scientific-revolutions-.point: Eventually, scientists encounter anomalies: results that the paradigm cannot explain. At first these are ignored or treated as errors. When anomalies accumulate or concern central issues, the field enters a crisis, and scientists begin to question basic assumptions. Kuhn cites the discovery of oxygen, which undermined the phlogiston theory of combustion, and problems in astronomy that preceded the Copernican revolution.

six-thinking-hats-02.cue: What do the white and red hats represent?
six-thinking-hats-02.point: The white hat focuses on information: facts, figures and what is known or needed, without interpretation. The red hat allows feelings, intuition and hunches to be expressed without justification. De Bono argues that emotions influence decisions anyway, so it's better to bring them into the open. Separating facts from feelings makes discussion clearer and more honest.

trillion-dollar-coach-03.also: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team; The Ideal Team Player
trillion-dollar-coach-03.cue: What is Campbell's approach to teams?
trillion-dollar-coach-03.point: Campbell believed teams come first. He focused on the team's success over individual achievements and worked on getting the right players, those with intelligence, work ethic, integrity and grit. He encouraged executives to work as a team, resolving conflicts and tensions, which he called the elephant in the room. He also helped teams solve the biggest problem first, rather than getting distracted.

the-compound-effect-01.point: Darren Hardy's principle that small, smart choices repeated consistently over time produce dramatic results. Like compound interest, the payoff is invisible at first and then grows exponentially; a penny doubled daily for 31 days becomes over $10 million. Eating 100 fewer calories a day or reading 30 minutes daily changes little this week but transforms a year. It also works in reverse with small bad habits.

radical-acceptance-01.also: The Gifts of Imperfection; Mindfulness in Plain English
radical-acceptance-01.point: Tara Brach, a psychologist and Buddhist meditation teacher, defines radical acceptance as clearly recognizing what we are feeling in the present moment and regarding that experience with compassion. Many people live in a trance of unworthiness, believing something is wrong with them. Radical acceptance means meeting our experience, including painful emotions, without judgment or resistance. Brach argues this is the path to healing and freedom.

who-will-cry-when-you-die-05.also: How Will You Measure Your Life?; The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
who-will-cry-when-you-die-05.cue: What does Sharma say about purpose and legacy?
who-will-cry-when-you-die-05.point: Sharma encourages readers to discover their calling and pursue it with passion. He suggests imagining your funeral and what you'd want people to say, then living accordingly. He recommends setting goals, continually learning and contributing to others. Legacy, he argues, is built through daily acts of service and character, not grand achievements alone. Sharma argues that a life lived this way leaves people better off for having known you.

sapiens-05.cue: What changed in human thinking with the Scientific Revolution?
sapiens-05.point: Four shifts. We admitted ignorance and began questioning what we thought we knew. We relied on observation and mathematics instead of sacred texts. We pursued knowledge for the power it gives, especially technology. And we began believing in progress, while our ancestors placed the golden age in the past. Francis Bacon's idea of judging knowledge by its usefulness tied science to technology, and war tightened that link.

the-100-startup-02.also: So Good They Can't Ignore You; Ikigai
the-100-startup-02.cue: What is convergence in Guillebeau's framework?
the-100-startup-02.point: Convergence is the overlap between what you are passionate about or skilled at and what other people want and will pay for. Passion alone is not enough; a hobby becomes a business only when it solves a problem for customers. Guillebeau also stresses skill transformation: many founders used related abilities, such as a teacher using communication skills to run online courses. Look at what people ask you for help with to find your convergence.

can-t-hurt-me-07.cue: Why does Goggins warn against settling into comfort after success?
can-t-hurt-me-07.point: He argues that achievements are temporary and that the moment you feel you have arrived, you begin to slide back. After each milestone he searched for a harder challenge, such as ultramarathons and a pull up world record, because staying uncomfortable keeps the mind sharp. He also stresses that there is no finish line for self improvement. The work of becoming who you want to be has to be renewed every day.

all-marketers-are-liars-05.cue: Why do first impressions matter so much in Godin's view?
all-marketers-are-liars-05.point: Godin argues consumers make up their minds almost instantly, based on small details, and then spend the rest of the time confirming their first judgment. A restaurant's smell, a website's design or a salesperson's handshake can set the story the customer tells. He cites Riedel wine glasses, whose elegant design convinces drinkers that wine tastes better. Marketers should design every early touchpoint to start the right story, since changing it later is very hard.

attached-03.cue: What is the anxious avoidant trap?
attached-03.point: Anxious and avoidant people often end up together, since the avoidant person's distance triggers the anxious person's attachment system, which can be mistaken for passion. The anxious partner pursues while the avoidant withdraws, creating a painful cycle. The authors argue this pairing is common because avoidant people are disproportionately available on the dating market. Recognizing the pattern can help people break it or choose differently.

predictably-irrational-10.cue: Why do honest people cheat, and how can you resist it?
predictably-irrational-10.point: Most people cheat a little while still seeing themselves as honest. Cheating is easier when it is one step removed from cash: people who would never steal a dollar will take pens from work or pad an expense report. Moral reminders reduce cheating; people asked to recall the Ten Commandments cheated less. Ask yourself whether you would take the equivalent amount of cash.

secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-03.also: The Magic of Thinking Big; Rich Dad's Cashflow Quadrant
secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-03.cue: What are some of Eker's wealth files?
secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-03.point: Eker lists seventeen ways rich and poor people think differently. Rich people believe they create their life, while poor people believe life happens to them. Rich people play to win money, while poor people play not to lose. Rich people focus on opportunities, admire other successful people and are willing to promote themselves. Rich people think big and act despite fear. Critics see these as broad generalizations.

think-like-a-rocket-scientist-06.cue: How do you overcome confirmation bias?
think-like-a-rocket-scientist-06.point: Scientists treat beliefs as hypotheses to be tested and actively try to prove them wrong. Most of us do the opposite, seeking evidence that supports what we already think and clinging to our stories, especially when they become part of our identity. Generate several competing hypotheses so you don't anchor on one, examine your beliefs as if they were someone else's and invite others to poke holes in them.

fast-food-nation-06.also: The Omnivore's Dilemma; How Not to Die
fast-food-nation-06.point: He calls for stronger food safety regulation, including the power to recall contaminated meat, better protection for meatpacking workers, limits on marketing to children, and support for small farmers and ranchers. He also argues consumers have power: by choosing not to buy fast food, people can push the industry to change. In later editions he noted some improvements, such as better beef testing, while many problems remained.

tools-of-titans-05.cue: What health practices does Tools of Titans highlight?
tools-of-titans-05.point: Ferriss shares routines from athletes and doctors, such as Jocko Willink's early workouts, Wim Hof's breathing techniques, cold exposure, fasting, ketogenic diets and strength training. He notes these practices vary in scientific support and should be approached with caution. The common thread is experimenting with self tracking and finding small, sustainable changes that improve energy and focus.

the-1-page-marketing-plan-04.also: Ogilvy on Advertising; How Brands Grow
the-1-page-marketing-plan-04.cue: Why does Dib favor direct response marketing over brand building?
the-1-page-marketing-plan-04.point: Large companies can afford brand advertising that builds awareness slowly, but small businesses need marketing that produces measurable responses quickly. Direct response marketing includes a specific call to action, tracks results, and aims to capture leads rather than impress people. Every campaign should be tested and measured so that money flows to what works. Dib recommends calculating customer lifetime value to know how much you can spend to acquire a customer.

inspired-02.also: Turn the Ship Around!; No Rules Rules
inspired-02.point: Cagan argues that instead of feature teams that build what they're told, companies need empowered product teams that are given problems to solve and held accountable for outcomes. Each team includes a product manager, a product designer and engineers working together from the start. Teams should be durable and cross functional, with ownership of a product area. Empowerment leads to better solutions and more motivated people.

the-hard-thing-about-hard-things-05.also: High Output Management; Leaders Eat Last
the-hard-thing-about-hard-things-05.cue: Why does Horowitz emphasize taking care of people, products and profits?
the-hard-thing-about-hard-things-05.point: He argues taking care of people comes first, since a good place to work enables everything else. He defines a good company as one where people can focus on their work, knowing that if they do their jobs well, good things will happen for them and the company. Training employees, having one on ones and setting clear expectations are key. Products and profits follow when people are well managed.

secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-02.also: You Are A Badass; The Psychology of Money
secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-02.cue: How is the money blueprint formed?
secrets-of-the-millionaire-mind-02.point: Eker identifies three influences: verbal programming, what you heard about money, such as money is the root of all evil; modeling, what you saw your parents do with money; and specific incidents, experiences involving money that shaped emotions. He suggests identifying these influences, understanding how they affect your behavior, and consciously choosing new beliefs that support wealth.

money-master-the-game-01.also: The Simple Path to Wealth; I Will Teach You to Be Rich
money-master-the-game-01.cue: What is Tony Robbins's goal in Money: Master the Game?
money-master-the-game-01.point: Robbins interviewed about fifty financial experts, including Ray Dalio, Jack Bogle and Warren Buffett, to distill a seven step plan for financial freedom. He argues that ordinary investors can reach security and independence by saving consistently, avoiding high fees, investing in low cost index funds and building an all weather portfolio. He frames money as a game with rules that most people never learn.

give-and-take-02.cue: Why do some givers succeed while others fail?
give-and-take-02.point: Grant distinguishes selfless givers, who help others at their own expense and burn out, from otherish givers, who care about others while also pursuing their own interests. Successful givers set boundaries, prioritize helping in ways that energize them, and are careful about takers. They chunk their giving into concentrated periods, which increases its impact on their well being.

21-lessons-for-the-21st-century-05.cue: How does Harari frame the immigration debate?
21-lessons-for-the-21st-century-05.point: He describes immigration as a deal with three terms. The host country admits immigrants. Immigrants adopt the host country's core norms and values. In return, once they assimilate, they become equal members. Supporters and opponents disagree about each term: whether admission is a duty or a favor, how much assimilation is required and how long full acceptance should take. Both sides raise legitimate points, which makes the debate hard to settle.

battlefield-of-the-mind-03.also: Extreme Ownership; The Road Less Traveled
battlefield-of-the-mind-03.point: Meyer uses the Israelites wandering in the wilderness for forty years as a metaphor for people stuck in destructive patterns. She lists mentalities such as "my future is determined by my past," "someone else is responsible for my problems," "I can't help it if I'm addicted," and "I don't want to wait." These attitudes keep people circling the same problems. Recognizing them is the first step toward entering what she calls the promised land.

essentialism-02.cue: Why do successful people often become less effective over time, according to McKeown?
essentialism-02.point: He calls it the clarity paradox. Clarity of purpose leads to success, success brings more options and requests, and saying yes to them diffuses the focus that created the success in the first place. Eventually the person is busy everywhere and excellent nowhere. Breaking the cycle requires returning to clarity: deciding what you will not do, even when the options are attractive, so your effort stays concentrated.

all-marketers-are-liars-01.cue: What is Seth Godin's main argument?
all-marketers-are-liars-01.point: Godin argues that consumers don't buy products; they buy stories they tell themselves. Successful marketers tell stories that match the worldview of their audience, which consumers then believe and spread. He says marketers aren't really liars; consumers are, because they convince themselves of stories that make them feel good. The book was later retitled All Marketers Tell Stories.

how-to-talk-to-anyone-02.cue: What are sticky eyes and the epoxy eyes technique?
how-to-talk-to-anyone-02.point: Lowndes suggests keeping your eyes on the other person a little longer than usual, even after they finish speaking, before slowly looking away. This conveys intense interest and warmth. With epoxy eyes, when in a group, you keep watching the person you want to impress even while someone else is speaking, so they notice you are focused on their reactions. She warns these techniques can feel intense and should be used with care.

the-god-delusion-02.also: The Selfish Gene; Brief Answers to the Big Questions
the-god-delusion-02.cue: What is Dawkins's Ultimate Boeing 747 argument?
the-god-delusion-02.point: Creationists argue complex life is as improbable as a hurricane assembling a Boeing 747. Dawkins turns this around: a designer capable of creating complex life would itself need to be even more complex and improbable, so invoking God doesn't solve the problem. Natural selection, by contrast, explains complexity through gradual, cumulative steps. He argues this makes God's existence highly unlikely.

ted-talks-the-official-ted-guide-to-publ.cue: Why does Anderson say public speaking matters more than ever?
ted-talks-the-official-ted-guide-to-publ.point: Anderson argues that online video has made public speaking a global force, since a great talk can reach millions. In an interconnected world, sharing ideas through speech is a powerful way to spread knowledge, inspire action and build understanding. He sees this as a revival of an ancient human practice of gathering around fires to share stories, now amplified by technology.

the-plant-paradox-02.also: How Not to Die; Why We Get Sick
the-plant-paradox-02.cue: What does Gundry recommend eating and avoiding?
the-plant-paradox-02.point: Gundry lists yes foods, such as leafy greens, cruciferous vegetables, avocados, olive oil, pasture raised meats and wild fish, and no foods, such as grains, legumes, nightshades, most fruit out of season and conventional dairy. He suggests pressure cooking beans to reduce lectins. His program begins with a three day cleanse. Critics note the diet is restrictive and lacks strong clinical evidence.

outliers-01.also: The Psychology of Money; David and Goliath
outliers-01.cue: What is the main argument of Outliers?
outliers-01.point: Malcolm Gladwell argues that extraordinary success is not just the result of individual talent and effort, but of hidden advantages, opportunities and cultural legacies. Outliers, people who achieve far beyond the norm, benefit from circumstances such as when and where they were born and the opportunities they had. Understanding these factors challenges the myth of the self made individual.

sell-or-be-sold-05.also: The Magic of Thinking Big; The Sales Bible
sell-or-be-sold-05.cue: What does Cardone say about attitude and self development?
sell-or-be-sold-05.point: Cardone believes salespeople must invest in themselves through daily learning, studying sales techniques and reading. He suggests surrounding yourself with positive, successful people and avoiding negative influences. Attitude affects every interaction, so salespeople must maintain enthusiasm even after rejection. He argues the best salespeople are always students of their craft. He frames sales skill as something built through daily practice rather than innate charm.

how-brands-grow-03.also: Made to Stick; The 1-Page Marketing Plan
how-brands-grow-03.cue: What are mental and physical availability?
how-brands-grow-03.point: Mental availability is how easily a brand comes to mind in buying situations, built by creating memory structures linked to category entry points, the cues that trigger a purchase. Physical availability is how easy the brand is to find and buy, through distribution and shelf presence. Sharp argues these two factors drive growth more than persuasive messaging or differentiation.

10-happier-04.cue: Why does Harris say meditation makes you 10 percent happier?
10-happier-04.point: He chose the modest claim deliberately to counter exaggerated promises of enlightenment. Meditation did not transform him into a serene monk. It made him somewhat calmer, less reactive and better at recovering from setbacks, which he considers a large return on a small time investment. He cites research linking meditation to reduced stress and changes in brain regions involved in attention and emotional regulation.

business-model-generation-05.also: The Innovator's Dilemma; Blue Ocean Strategy
business-model-generation-05.cue: How does the canvas help established companies?
business-model-generation-05.point: Established firms can use the canvas to assess their current model, identify threats from disruptive competitors and explore new models. The authors suggest evaluating each building block's strengths and weaknesses. They also discuss managing multiple business models within one organization, which can create conflict, and options like separating new models into autonomous units, a theme connected to Clayton Christensen's research.

the-oz-principle-01.also: Extreme Ownership; The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
the-oz-principle-01.cue: What is The Oz Principle about?
the-oz-principle-01.point: Roger Connors, Tom Smith and Craig Hickman argue that accountability is the key to individual and organizational results. Drawing on The Wizard of Oz, they note that Dorothy and her companions searched for something they already had. Similarly, people already have the power to achieve results but often get stuck below the line, blaming others and making excuses. Rising above the line means taking ownership.

the-road-less-traveled-04.also: The Purpose Driven Life; The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
the-road-less-traveled-04.cue: What does Peck say about growth and religion?
the-road-less-traveled-04.point: Peck argues spiritual growth involves expanding our worldview, which may include religion. He sees people's religions as their maps of the world, which should evolve as they mature. He describes stages of spiritual development, from chaotic to formal to skeptical to mystical. Peck, a psychiatrist who later embraced Christianity, sees psychotherapy and spiritual growth as closely related.

the-art-of-the-deal-03.cue: How does the book describe the use of publicity?
the-art-of-the-deal-03.point: Trump argues that controversy and bold claims attract media attention, which serves as free advertising. He describes using truthful hyperbole, his term for exaggeration that plays to people's fantasies, to promote projects. Schwartz later regretted the phrase. Trump writes that the press is always hungry for good stories, and being different or outrageous gets covered. Critics see this as a defense of misleading claims.

the-happiness-advantage-01.point: Shawn Achor, a researcher who studied happiness at Harvard, argues that most people believe success leads to happiness, but research suggests the reverse: happiness leads to success. Positive brains perform better, are more creative, and are more resilient. Achor describes seven principles for leveraging this advantage at work. He argues happiness is not a fixed trait but can be cultivated through practices.

emotional-intelligence-03.also: Mindfulness in Plain English; Emotional Intelligence 2.0
emotional-intelligence-03.cue: Why is self awareness the foundation of emotional intelligence?
emotional-intelligence-03.point: Self awareness means recognizing feelings as they happen. People who are aware of their emotions can manage them better and make better personal decisions, such as whom to marry or which job to take. Goleman describes styles: self aware people, those engulfed by emotions, and those who accept their moods without trying to change them. Mindfulness of emotions creates the space needed to choose responses.

thinking-in-systems-02.point: A stock is anything you can count or measure at a moment, like water in a bathtub, money in a bank account or the world's population. Flows change the stock over time: inflows raise it and outflows lower it. Because flows take time to act, stocks change slowly and act as buffers. A savings account lets you survive a lost job, and a workforce cannot be retrained overnight.

think-like-a-monk-05.cue: What meditation practices does Shetty recommend?
think-like-a-monk-05.point: Shetty describes three practices: breathwork, which calms the body and mind; visualization, which helps envision goals and heal from past experiences; and mantra chanting, repeating a sound or phrase to focus the mind. He suggests starting with just a few minutes a day and building up. Regular practice, he argues, trains the mind to be calmer, clearer and more compassionate.

why-we-sleep-06.cue: Which health problems has poor sleep been linked to?
why-we-sleep-06.point: Walker connects chronic short sleep with heart disease, diabetes, weight gain, weakened immunity, some cancers, reduced fertility, Alzheimer's and shorter life. During deep sleep the brain's cleaning system flushes out proteins linked to Alzheimer's. Many of these findings are correlational, and critics have challenged some of Walker's claims, yet experiments do show sleep loss raising blood pressure and disrupting blood sugar control.

make-it-stick-01.cue: Why is rereading a weak way to learn, and what works better?
make-it-stick-01.point: Rereading feels productive because the material becomes familiar, yet familiarity fades quickly and is easily mistaken for mastery. Retrieval practice works far better: anything that forces you to pull an idea from memory, such as flashcards, self-quizzing or reflecting on how you handled a problem. Each act of recall strengthens the memory and shows you what you actually know and what you only recognize.

the-magic-of-thinking-big-03.also: The Confidence Code; The War of Art
the-magic-of-thinking-big-03.cue: How does Schwartz suggest overcoming fear?
the-magic-of-thinking-big-03.point: Action cures fear, while indecision and postponement fertilize it. Schwartz suggests isolating your fear and taking constructive action against it. He also recommends building confidence by sitting in front, practicing eye contact, walking faster, speaking up in meetings, and smiling. These behaviors change how others see you and how you see yourself. Managing memory, focusing on positive experiences, also builds confidence.

the-defining-decade-06.cue: What relationship mistakes does Jay warn twenty-somethings against?
the-defining-decade-06.point: Dating down, meaning staying with someone you have outgrown, often driven by old stories about not being good enough. Sliding into cohabitation without deciding, since couples who move in together before getting engaged are more likely to divorce, partly because the costs of leaving pile up. Look for similar personalities, using the Big Five traits, and consider the family you would be joining.

surrounded-by-idiots-05.also: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team; Thanks for the Feedback
surrounded-by-idiots-05.cue: How can colors help teams and feedback?
surrounded-by-idiots-05.point: Teams benefit from a mix of colors, since each brings strengths: Reds drive action, Yellows generate ideas, Greens build cohesion and Blues ensure quality. Conflict often arises when colors clash, like a Red pushing a Blue to decide quickly. Erikson suggests giving feedback in ways each color can hear, such as being factual with Blues and gentle with Greens. Self awareness of your own color reduces blind spots.

the-22-immutable-laws-of-marketing-02.cue: What is the Law of the Category?
the-22-immutable-laws-of-marketing-02.point: If you can't be first in a category, create a new category you can be first in. When Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, she became famous despite not being first overall. Instead of asking how your product is better, ask what category it is first in. Promoting the new category, rather than the brand, helps establish leadership.

to-sell-is-human-03.also: Quiet: The Power of Introverts; Give and Take
to-sell-is-human-03.cue: Why does Pink say ambiverts make the best salespeople?
to-sell-is-human-03.point: Common wisdom holds that extroverts make the best salespeople. Pink cites research by Adam Grant showing that ambiverts, people between introversion and extroversion, outperformed both. Extroverts may talk too much and listen too little, while introverts may be too reluctant to make the sale. Ambiverts know when to speak and when to listen. Most people are ambiverts, so most can sell effectively.

the-e-myth-revisited-04.cue: What is the business development process?
the-e-myth-revisited-04.point: Gerber outlines seven steps: define your primary aim, what you want your life to look like; your strategic objective, what the business must achieve to serve that aim; your organizational strategy, with an organization chart of roles; your management strategy, systems for producing results; your people strategy, communicating the game to employees; your marketing strategy, focused on customers; and your systems strategy, integrating it all.

business-adventures-04.also: The Smartest Guys in the Room; Leadership and Self-Deception
business-adventures-04.cue: What lesson does Brooks draw from the General Electric price fixing scandal?
business-adventures-04.point: In 1961, executives at GE and other electrical equipment makers were convicted of illegally fixing prices. Brooks explores how they rationalized behavior that violated both law and company policy. GE's leadership claimed ignorance, and communication failures meant that rules were understood differently at different levels. Brooks highlights how organizations can send mixed signals, allowing employees to believe illegal conduct is tacitly expected.

the-black-swan-04.cue: Why is predicting even the past so hard?
the-black-swan-04.point: Imagine an ice cube melting on a table. You can predict the shape of the puddle. Now look at a puddle and try to work out what made it: an ice cube, a spilled glass or something else. Countless causes produce the same result, so working backward is guesswork. Historians explaining events face the same problem, which is why tidy historical explanations deserve suspicion.

zero-to-one-01.cue: What does Peter Thiel mean by going from zero to one?
zero-to-one-01.point: Peter Thiel, cofounder of PayPal and an early Facebook investor, distinguishes horizontal progress, copying things that work, going from 1 to n, from vertical progress, doing new things, going from 0 to 1. Globalization spreads existing ideas, while technology creates new ones. He argues the future depends on creating new technologies, and that startups are the best vehicles for doing so. The book grew out of his Stanford lectures.

positioning-04.cue: What do Ries and Trout say about names and line extensions?
positioning-04.point: A good name is crucial, since it's the first point of contact with the mind. Names should suggest the product's benefit or position. Ries and Trout warn against line extensions, using a successful brand name for a different product, which blurs the position. They also criticize generic, initial based names like corporate acronyms, which fail to communicate anything memorable.

the-smartest-guys-in-the-room-04.also: The Shock Doctrine; Skin in the Game
the-smartest-guys-in-the-room-04.cue: How did Enron manipulate energy markets?
the-smartest-guys-in-the-room-04.point: During the California energy crisis of 2000 to 2001, Enron traders exploited flaws in the deregulated market, creating artificial shortages and manipulating prices. Recorded calls showed traders joking about the crisis. Californians faced blackouts and soaring prices. The scandal showed how poorly designed deregulation allowed manipulation, and how Enron's culture rewarded profit at any cost.

mountains-beyond-mountains-01.also: The Emperor of All Maladies; The Bottom Billion
mountains-beyond-mountains-01.point: Tracy Kidder's book profiles Paul Farmer, a physician and anthropologist who cofounded Partners In Health to provide medical care to the world's poorest people, starting in rural Haiti. Farmer combined Harvard medical training with a deep commitment to social justice. He believed that health care is a human right and that the poor deserve the same quality of care as the rich. He died in 2022 in Rwanda.

grit-02.cue: What did the West Point Beast Barracks study reveal?
grit-02.point: West Point admits cadets using a Whole Candidate Score that weighs grades, test scores, leadership and fitness, yet about one in twenty still quit during the brutal first summer. Duckworth gave incoming cadets a short Grit Scale questionnaire. Their grit scores predicted who would make it through far better than the admissions score did. Staying power in a hard environment depended more on persistence than on the impressive credentials that got them admitted.

the-fifth-agreement-05.cue: What do the Ruizes mean by the dream of the planet?
the-fifth-agreement-05.point: The authors describe the dream of the planet as the collective beliefs society teaches through domestication, such as family, school and culture. People learn to judge themselves and live by others' standards. Awareness of this dream allows people to choose which beliefs to keep, breaking free from fear. Ultimately they describe a dream of heaven, living with love and acceptance.

the-new-jim-crow-04.also: Hillbilly Elegy; The Color of Law
the-new-jim-crow-04.cue: What happens to people after prison?
the-new-jim-crow-04.point: Alexander argues that the real punishment often begins after release. People with felony records can be legally denied jobs, housing, food stamps and student aid, and in many states lose the right to vote or serve on juries. They also face fines and fees. These barriers push many back toward crime and prison. She calls this a closed circuit of perpetual marginality.

nudge-05.cue: How do social influences nudge behavior?
nudge-05.point: People strongly follow what others do. Telling residents that most of their neighbors pay taxes on time increased compliance, and showing households how their energy use compares to neighbors reduced consumption. Social influence works through information, since others' actions signal what is wise, and through peer pressure. The authors warn that highlighting bad behavior, such as "many people steal petrified wood," can backfire by making it seem normal.

the-whole-brain-child-01.cue: What is The Whole-Brain Child about?
the-whole-brain-child-01.point: Neuropsychiatrist Daniel Siegel and parenting expert Tina Payne Bryson explain how a child's developing brain works and offer twelve strategies to help children integrate different parts of their brain. Integration means helping parts of the brain work together, such as left and right, upstairs and downstairs. An integrated brain leads to better emotional regulation, decision making and relationships. Everyday challenges become opportunities to support development.

the-purpose-driven-life-05.also: Lost Connections; The Road to Character
the-purpose-driven-life-05.cue: What does Warren say about community and character?
the-purpose-driven-life-05.point: Warren emphasizes that people are meant to live in community, sharing life with other believers, and that isolation is harmful. Real fellowship involves authenticity, mutuality, sympathy and mercy. He argues character develops through trials and temptations, which test and strengthen faith. Spiritual growth is gradual and requires commitment, not instant transformation. He encourages readers to join a small group where people know and support each other.

elon-musk-02.point: After selling PayPal, Musk wanted to inspire public interest in space and eventually make humans a multiplanetary species, beginning with Mars. When he found existing rockets too expensive, he founded SpaceX in 2002 to build cheaper rockets in house. The first three Falcon 1 launches failed, nearly bankrupting the company, but the fourth succeeded in 2008. NASA then awarded a major contract, saving SpaceX.

way-of-the-wolf-01.also: The Psychology of Selling; Sell or Be Sold
way-of-the-wolf-01.cue: What is Jordan Belfort's Straight Line System?
way-of-the-wolf-01.point: Belfort, the former stockbroker portrayed in The Wolf of Wall Street, who served prison time for securities fraud, presents his sales method. The Straight Line System holds that every sale follows a straight line from the opening to the close, and the salesperson's job is to keep the prospect on that line, steering back when they veer off. He argues sales skills can be taught and used ethically, despite his own past.

the-black-swan-05.cue: Why are many great discoveries accidents?
the-black-swan-05.point: Breakthroughs often come from luck and tinkering rather than planned research. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin because he left bacterial cultures out while on vacation and came back to find mold killing the bacteria. Because the biggest discoveries are unpredictable, rigid long-term plans miss them. Exposure to many small chances and attention to surprises matter more than precise forecasts.

the-lean-startup-02.point: Learning backed by data from real customer experiments. Bad learning means executing a plan, watching it succeed or fail and then inventing an explanation afterward. Validated learning means stating a clear hypothesis, designing an experiment to test it and measuring results. A startup's progress is measured in validated learning about what customers want and will pay for, not in features shipped or hours worked.

so-good-they-can-t-ignore-you-05.cue: When should you quit a job instead of building skills there?
so-good-they-can-t-ignore-you-05.point: Leave when the job offers few chances to build rare and valuable skills, when it focuses on something you think is useless or harmful to the world, or when it forces you to work with people you dislike. You could in theory gain career capital in such a place, but you would be unlikely to stay long enough for it to pay off.

the-ideal-team-player-05.also: The Culture Code; Death by Meeting
the-ideal-team-player-05.cue: What is the fable in The Ideal Team Player about?
the-ideal-team-player-05.point: The fable follows Jeff Shanley, who takes over his uncle's construction company, Valley Builders. Facing two major projects requiring many new hires and a tense culture, he and his leaders discover that their best people share humility, hunger and people smarts. They build hiring and development processes around these virtues. The story shows how culture can be deliberately shaped through people decisions.

the-ideal-team-player-04.cue: How can managers develop team players?
the-ideal-team-player-04.point: Lencioni suggests assessing current employees against the three virtues and having honest conversations about gaps. People can develop these virtues if they are willing. Managers should coach employees, give feedback and model the behaviors. Teams can embed the virtues into performance reviews and culture. Those who refuse to improve may need to leave for the team's sake.

the-absolutely-true-diary-of-a-part-time.cue: Why does Arnold leave the reservation school?
the-absolutely-true-diary-of-a-part-time.point: Arnold throws a textbook in anger when he discovers it is the same book his mother used decades earlier, illustrating how little the reservation school has. His teacher, Mr. P, visits him and urges him to leave, saying the reservation teaches people to give up. Arnold decides to attend Reardan, a wealthier white school, to seek a better future, even though his community sees it as betrayal.

hooked-04.cue: Why are variable rewards so compelling?
hooked-04.point: Predictable rewards don't create cravings; you don't crave turning on your faucet. Unpredictable rewards, like a slot machine, spike dopamine and keep us coming back for the next hit. Eyal describes three kinds. Rewards of the tribe come from social validation like likes. Rewards of the hunt come from finding resources or information, like scrolling a feed. Rewards of the self come from mastery and completion, like clearing an inbox.

who-not-how-05.cue: What are the benefits of the who not how mindset?
who-not-how-05.point: Sullivan and Hardy argue that adopting this mindset increases freedom of time, money, relationships and purpose. You can pursue bigger goals and create more impact. Relationships become collaborative rather than transactional. It also reduces stress, since you're not trying to do everything alone. They suggest starting small by identifying one task you can hand off to a who this week.

the-five-people-you-meet-in-heaven-01.cue: What is the premise of The Five People You Meet in Heaven?
the-five-people-you-meet-in-heaven-01.point: Mitch Albom's novel follows Eddie, an elderly maintenance worker at a seaside amusement park, who dies on his 83rd birthday trying to save a girl from a falling ride. He awakens in the afterlife, where he meets five people whose lives intersected with his, some of whom he barely knew. Each teaches him a lesson about the meaning of his life, which he had considered dull and wasted.

sex-at-dawn-02.also: The Selfish Gene; Why We Get Sick
sex-at-dawn-02.cue: What evidence do the authors cite?
sex-at-dawn-02.point: Ryan and Jethá point to our closest relatives, bonobos and chimpanzees, which are not monogamous. They cite anatomical features, ethnographic accounts of foraging societies with flexible relationships, and the widespread human interest in novelty. They argue modern patterns like infidelity and divorce reflect a mismatch between evolved desires and social norms. Critics argue they selectively interpret data and overlook evidence of pair bonding.

the-white-man-s-burden-03.also: Black Box Thinking; Measure What Matters
the-white-man-s-burden-03.cue: Why does Easterly emphasize feedback and accountability?
the-white-man-s-burden-03.point: In markets, customers give feedback by buying or not buying, so businesses adapt. In aid, the people served often have no voice, and agencies answer to donors rather than recipients. Easterly argues this lack of feedback leads to failed projects. He calls for evaluating programs rigorously and holding agencies accountable for measurable results, such as delivering medicines or bed nets.

on-writing-well-02.cue: What does Zinsser mean by clutter?
on-writing-well-02.point: Clutter is the disease of American writing, Zinsser argues: unnecessary words, long phrases where short ones would do, and euphemisms that obscure meaning. Examples include saying "at this point in time" instead of "now." He recommends examining every word and cutting anything that doesn't do useful work. Simplicity requires discipline but makes writing clearer and more persuasive.

12-rules-for-life-03.cue: Why does Peterson say to compare yourself to who you were yesterday?
12-rules-for-life-03.point: Comparing yourself to others is demoralizing, since there is always someone better at something, and the comparisons ignore their hidden costs. Instead, measure progress against your past self. Pick small, achievable improvements each day and ask what you could do to make life slightly better. Incremental progress compounds over time. This also requires honesty about your own shortcomings, rather than resentment of other people's success.

man-s-search-for-meaning-03.also: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People; Meditations
man-s-search-for-meaning-03.cue: What is the last of the human freedoms?
man-s-search-for-meaning-03.point: Frankl argues that everything can be taken from a person except one thing: the freedom to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances. Even in the camps, some prisoners chose to comfort others and give away their last piece of bread. Between stimulus and response there is a space, in which lies our power to choose our response. This freedom gives life meaning even in suffering.

extreme-ownership-02.also: Good to Great; Leaders Eat Last
extreme-ownership-02.cue: What does "There are no bad teams, only bad leaders" mean?
extreme-ownership-02.point: Willink describes a SEAL training exercise in which a boat crew repeatedly came last. When its leader was swapped with the leader of the winning crew, the losing crew began winning. The team members were the same; only leadership changed. Leaders set standards: what they tolerate becomes the norm. Teams take on the attitudes of their leaders.

blink-03.cue: When do snap judgments go wrong?
blink-03.point: Our unconscious can be biased by stereotypes and irrelevant cues. Gladwell describes the Warren Harding error: Harding was elected president largely because he looked presidential, yet proved ineffective. The Implicit Association Test shows many people hold unconscious associations they consciously reject. Car salespeople who judged customers by appearance offered worse deals to women and Black buyers. Snap judgments are only as good as the experience behind them.

the-dichotomy-of-leadership-01.also: Extreme Ownership; Turn the Ship Around!
the-dichotomy-of-leadership-01.cue: What is the main idea of The Dichotomy of Leadership?
the-dichotomy-of-leadership-01.point: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin, former Navy SEAL officers who wrote Extreme Ownership, argue that leadership requires balancing opposing forces. A leader must be confident but not cocky, aggressive but not reckless, disciplined but not rigid, and close to the team but not so close that they lose authority. Leaning too far toward either extreme causes failure. The key is awareness of where you stand and adjusting as situations change.

thank-you-for-being-late-05.also: The Bottom Billion; Thinking in Systems
thank-you-for-being-late-05.cue: How does Friedman connect acceleration to geopolitics?
thank-you-for-being-late-05.point: Friedman argues the world is divided between a world of order, where countries benefit from globalization, and a world of disorder, where states fail under pressure from climate stress, population growth and technology. He calls for policies that help vulnerable regions, strengthen resilience and manage migration. Using ecological thinking, he argues healthy systems are diverse, adaptive and interconnected.

can-t-hurt-me-06.cue: What is taking souls, in Goggins's language?
can-t-hurt-me-06.point: Taking someone's soul means outperforming expectations so completely that you break a rival's or an instructor's belief that you can be beaten. Goggins used it during SEAL training to stay motivated by pushing harder than anyone expected, especially when instructors tried to make candidates quit. Later he redirected the idea inward, competing against his own past limits. It is a tactic for turning a contest or hostile environment into energy instead of letting it drain you.

creativity-inc-06.cue: What did Catmull learn from Steve Jobs?
creativity-inc-06.point: Jobs bought Pixar from Lucasfilm in 1986 and funded it through years of losses. Catmull describes Jobs evolving from an abrasive leader into a more empathetic partner who learned to trust Pixar's creative teams. Jobs pushed for candor and quality, and his design of Pixar's headquarters encouraged chance encounters among employees. The relationship showed how leaders can grow over time.

scaling-up-01.point: Verne Harnish, founder of the Entrepreneurs' Organization, presents tools for growing companies, an update of his earlier book Mastering the Rockefeller Habits. He organizes them around four decisions every company must get right: people, strategy, execution and cash. He provides one page tools to help leadership teams align and grow. The book draws on the habits of John D. Rockefeller and successful growth companies.

lean-in-02.cue: What does Sandberg mean by sitting at the table?
lean-in-02.point: Sandberg describes a meeting where women took seats on the side of the room rather than at the main table, signaling they saw themselves as observers. She argues women often underestimate their abilities and suffer from impostor syndrome, while men tend to overestimate theirs. Sitting at the table means claiming your place, speaking up, and acting as if you belong, even when you feel unsure.

the-smartest-guys-in-the-room-05.cue: What were the consequences of the Enron scandal?
the-smartest-guys-in-the-room-05.point: Skilling was convicted of fraud and conspiracy and sentenced to prison. Founder Ken Lay was convicted but died before sentencing. Fastow pleaded guilty and testified. The scandal led to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which strengthened corporate accountability, required executives to certify financial statements and created stricter auditing rules. Enron became a symbol of corporate greed and fraud.

lean-in-03.cue: How does the likeability penalty affect women?
lean-in-03.point: Research shows that success and likeability are positively correlated for men but negatively correlated for women. In the Heidi and Howard study, students rated an identical case about a successful entrepreneur; when the name was Heidi, she was seen as less likeable and selfish. Women who negotiate assertively or show ambition face social backlash. Sandberg suggests women negotiate by framing requests around communal concerns.

primal-leadership-01.cue: What is the main idea of Primal Leadership?
primal-leadership-01.point: Daniel Goleman, Richard Boyatzis and Annie McKee argue that the primal task of leadership is emotional: leaders shape the emotional climate of their groups. Because emotions are contagious, a leader's mood spreads to others and affects performance. Leaders who create resonance, a positive emotional tone, bring out the best in people, while those who create dissonance drain energy. Emotional intelligence is therefore central to effective leadership.

on-writing-02.point: King says writers need a toolbox with several levels. On top are vocabulary and grammar. Use the first word that comes to mind if it is appropriate, and avoid dressing up vocabulary to sound impressive. Below that are elements of style: avoid passive voice and adverbs, which King says are not your friends. The paragraph, not the sentence, is the basic unit of writing, and good paragraphs give writing rhythm.

sex-at-dawn-05.also: The Righteous Mind; Merchants of Doubt
sex-at-dawn-05.cue: How has Sex at Dawn been received?
sex-at-dawn-05.point: The book became a bestseller and sparked debate. Supporters praised it for challenging assumptions about human nature. Critics, including anthropologist Lynn Saxon in her rebuttal Sex at Dusk, argued the authors misrepresented research, ignored contrary evidence and relied on cherry picked examples. Most evolutionary researchers view human mating as flexible, involving both pair bonding and other strategies, rather than one natural pattern.

merchants-of-doubt-01.point: People or organizations who make settled science look uncertain when its findings threaten their agenda, usually to delay regulation. The tobacco industry pioneered the playbook when research linked smoking to cancer. The same tactics were later used against science on acid rain, the ozone hole, secondhand smoke and climate change, often by the same small group of well-connected Cold War physicists like Fred Seitz and Fred Singer.

blitzscaling-01.also: Zero to One; Crossing the Chasm
blitzscaling-01.point: Reid Hoffman, cofounder of LinkedIn, and Chris Yeh define blitzscaling as prioritizing speed over efficiency in an environment of uncertainty. When winner take most markets emerge, the first company to reach scale often dominates. Blitzscaling means accepting high costs, chaos and risk to grow faster than competitors. It is not right for every business, only where speed creates lasting advantages like network effects.

sapiens-01.cue: What are the four revolutions that shaped human history?
sapiens-01.point: The Cognitive Revolution, about 70,000 years ago, gave Homo sapiens new language abilities. The Agricultural Revolution, about 10,000 years ago, turned foragers into farmers. The Scientific Revolution of the last 500 years taught us to admit ignorance and seek new powers. The Industrial Revolution unlocked new energy and made consumption a virtue. Together they explain how an unremarkable ape came to dominate the planet.

what-you-do-is-who-you-are-04.also: Man's Search for Meaning; Turn the Ship Around!
what-you-do-is-who-you-are-04.cue: What does Shaka Senghor teach about culture?
what-you-do-is-who-you-are-04.point: Shaka Senghor served nineteen years in prison for murder and transformed himself and his fellow prisoners' culture. He changed the prison culture by setting an example of nonviolence and education, and showing how changing personal behavior can influence others. Horowitz uses his story to show that culture can change even in the toughest environments when leaders model new behaviors.

the-art-of-thinking-clearly-01.also: Thinking, Fast and Slow; Predictably Irrational
the-art-of-thinking-clearly-01.cue: What is The Art of Thinking Clearly?
the-art-of-thinking-clearly-01.point: Rolf Dobelli, a Swiss writer, presents 99 short chapters describing cognitive biases and logical errors that distort decisions. He argues that we cannot eliminate them entirely, but recognizing them helps us avoid costly mistakes. The book draws heavily on research in behavioral economics and psychology. Dobelli recommends knowing what you don't want to do, since avoiding stupidity is easier than seeking brilliance.

the-12-week-year-02.cue: Why must your goals connect to a compelling vision?
the-12-week-year-02.point: Execution is hard, so you need an emotional reason to push through discomfort. Start with a long-term vision of the life you want across your personal, professional, financial and relational life, big enough to feel almost impossible. Then set what must happen in the next three years, and finally one or two goals for the coming 12 weeks. As you build a plan, belief moves from impossible to possible to probable to inevitable.

the-selfish-gene-05.also: The God Delusion; The Righteous Mind
the-selfish-gene-05.cue: Does Dawkins argue that humans must be selfish?
the-selfish-gene-05.point: No. Dawkins emphasizes that understanding the selfish gene does not justify selfish behavior. Humans are unique in being able to rebel against their genes through culture and foresight. We can deliberately cultivate generosity and cooperation even though our genes are selfish. He notes the theory describes how evolution works, not how we ought to behave, which is a moral question.

blue-ocean-strategy-03.cue: What are the paths to finding a blue ocean?
blue-ocean-strategy-03.point: Look across alternative industries that serve the same goal in different ways. Look at what makes customers trade up or down between price tiers. Look at different buyers in the chain, such as end users versus purchasers. Look at complementary products and what happens before and after use. Shift between functional and emotional appeal, follow clear trends to their conclusion and study noncustomers who stay out of the market.

building-a-storybrand-04.cue: How should a brand position itself as the guide?
building-a-storybrand-04.point: Guides show empathy, by understanding the customer's pain, and authority, through testimonials, statistics, awards and logos of clients. A guide is never the hero, like Yoda guiding Luke Skywalker. Brands that position themselves as heroes compete with customers for attention. Expressing empathy with a phrase like "we understand how frustrating it is" builds trust quickly.

digital-minimalism-08.cue: What practical steps help you resist the attention economy?
digital-minimalism-08.point: Delete social media apps from your phone and use the web versions only when needed. Turn your devices into single-purpose tools with blockers like Freedom. Use social media like a professional, following a small number of accounts. Shift to slow media by reading one reliable news source once a day. The most drastic step is switching to a basic phone that only calls and texts.

emotional-intelligence-02.also: The Chimp Paradox; Thinking, Fast and Slow
emotional-intelligence-02.point: The amygdala, part of the brain's emotional system, can trigger a powerful reaction before the rational neocortex has fully processed a situation. Goleman calls this an emotional hijacking, which explains outbursts of rage or panic we later regret. The amygdala evolved to respond quickly to threats, which once aided survival. Recognizing when you are being hijacked, and pausing to let the rational brain catch up, prevents many bad decisions.

the-21-irrefutable-laws-of-leadership-07.also: Good to Great; Built to Last
the-21-irrefutable-laws-of-leadership-07.cue: What is the Law of Legacy?
the-21-irrefutable-laws-of-leadership-07.point: A leader's lasting value is measured by succession. Maxwell argues the best leaders build organizations that thrive after they leave, by developing other leaders and creating a strong culture. He contrasts Roberto Goizueta at Coca Cola, who prepared successors well, with leaders whose companies collapsed after they departed. Leaders should think early about what they want to leave behind and invest in people who will carry it forward.

the-culture-code-04.also: Start With Why; Made to Stick
the-culture-code-04.cue: How do successful groups establish purpose?
the-culture-code-04.point: Groups create purpose through narratives: simple, repeated stories that define who they are and what they are trying to do. Coyle describes how high purpose environments use catchphrases and heuristics, like the restaurant team at Danny Meyer's establishments using sayings that capture their values. Leaders should name and rank priorities, be ten times clearer than they think necessary, and embrace catchphrases that turn values into behavior.

to-sell-is-human-02.also: Never Split the Difference; Give and Take
to-sell-is-human-02.cue: What are the new ABCs of selling?
to-sell-is-human-02.point: Pink replaces Always Be Closing with three qualities: Attunement, Buoyancy and Clarity. Attunement is bringing your actions and outlook into harmony with others, through perspective taking and strategic mimicry. Buoyancy is staying afloat amid rejection, through interrogative self talk and positive explanatory style. Clarity is helping others see their situations in fresh ways and identifying problems they didn't know they had.

pitch-anything-05.also: Made to Stick; The Charisma Myth
pitch-anything-05.cue: Why does Klaff emphasize intrigue and eradicating neediness?
pitch-anything-05.point: Intrigue keeps the croc brain engaged by introducing novelty and tension, such as a short story about a problem you faced under time pressure. Neediness, by contrast, triggers avoidance, since it signals weakness and risk. Klaff advises wanting nothing from the buyer, focusing only on things you do well, and announcing that you are about to leave. These behaviors make the pitcher appear valuable and confident.

scaling-up-05.point: Harnish argues growth consumes cash, and many growing companies fail because they run out of money despite being profitable. He suggests improving the cash conversion cycle, the time between paying for inputs and collecting from customers, through measures like faster billing, better payment terms and reducing inventory. Having cash reserves gives flexibility and resilience.

primal-leadership-04.cue: How can leaders develop emotional intelligence?
primal-leadership-04.point: The authors describe a process of self directed learning with five discoveries: identifying your ideal self, your vision of who you want to be; recognizing your real self, how others see you; creating a learning agenda to close the gaps; experimenting with new behaviors and practicing them; and building supportive relationships that help you change. Leaders must practice new habits repeatedly, since emotional skills reside in the brain's limbic system.

make-your-bed-01.cue: Why does Admiral McRaven say to make your bed?
make-your-bed-01.point: William McRaven, a retired Navy SEAL admiral, expanded his 2014 University of Texas commencement speech into this book of ten lessons from SEAL training. The first lesson: if you make your bed every morning, you will have accomplished the first task of the day. It gives you a small sense of pride and encourages you to do another task. If you have a miserable day, you will come home to a bed that is made.

black-box-thinking-02.cue: Why does healthcare learn more slowly than aviation, according to Syed?
black-box-thinking-02.point: In healthcare, mistakes have historically been covered up or rationalized, often to protect reputations and avoid lawsuits. Syed tells the story of Elaine Bromiley, who died during routine surgery after doctors fixated on a failing procedure. Her husband, an airline pilot, pushed for open investigation, which led to improvements. A culture of blame discourages reporting and learning.

the-war-of-art-01.cue: What is Resistance, according to Steven Pressfield?
the-war-of-art-01.point: Pressfield, a novelist, names the force that stops people from doing creative work Resistance. It shows up as procrastination, distraction, self doubt, fear and rationalization whenever we try to write, start a business, exercise or pursue any calling. Resistance is universal, internal and relentless. The more important the work is to our growth, the more Resistance we feel, so it can serve as a compass.

capitalism-and-freedom-03.cue: What did Friedman propose for education?
capitalism-and-freedom-03.point: Friedman argued that while society benefits from an educated public, which justifies government funding, it does not follow that government must run schools. He proposed school vouchers, giving parents a set amount per child to spend at any approved school, public or private. Competition, he argued, would improve quality and give poorer families choices that wealthier families already have. Vouchers remain controversial, with critics citing effects on public school funding and equity.

fast-food-nation-01.also: The Omnivore's Dilemma; The China Study
fast-food-nation-01.cue: What is Fast Food Nation about?
fast-food-nation-01.point: Eric Schlosser's 2001 investigation examines how the fast food industry transformed American diet, landscape, economy and culture. Beginning with the founders of chains like McDonald's and Carl's Jr. in postwar Southern California, he traces how fast food's model of uniformity and low cost reshaped agriculture, meatpacking and labor. He argues the industry's success came with hidden costs to workers, health, small farmers and the environment.

dare-to-lead-04.cue: What is armored leadership, and how do you reduce it on a team?
dare-to-lead-04.point: When people avoid vulnerability, they armor up with perfectionism, cynicism, blame, refusing accountability or using fear and power to control others. Leaders reduce armor by first noticing when they reward it, for example praising someone for never making a mistake. Next, name defensive behavior directly and explore what is driving it. Then publicly recognize people who ask for help, own mistakes and pair criticism with contributions.

the-4-hour-body-02.also: The Hacker's Diet; How Not to Die
the-4-hour-body-02.cue: What is the slow carb diet?
the-4-hour-body-02.point: Ferriss's slow carb diet has five rules: avoid white carbohydrates such as bread, rice and potatoes; eat the same few meals repeatedly; don't drink calories; don't eat fruit; and take one cheat day a week. Meals combine protein, legumes and vegetables. He argues the cheat day prevents metabolic slowdown and keeps the diet sustainable. Nutrition experts view it as a low glycemic diet with some unproven claims.
