hyperfocus-05.point: People working at computers are interrupted or switch tasks about every 40 seconds, partly because novelty gives the brain a hit of dopamine. Make distractions inconvenient by putting your phone in another room or disconnecting from the internet. Schedule email and meetings and give them focused attention too. When an unavoidable interruption comes, note what you were doing so you can return to it.

grit-01.cue: What is grit, according to Angela Duckworth?
grit-01.point: Grit is the combination of passion and perseverance applied to a long-term goal. Passion means staying devoted to the same top-level goal for years instead of jumping between interests. Perseverance means continuing to work hard after setbacks and boredom set in. Duckworth found that this combination predicts outstanding achievement better than raw talent, because people with grit keep improving long after others have stopped trying.

the-life-changing-magic-of-tidying-up-05.cue: How does tidying change people's lives, according to Kondo?
the-life-changing-magic-of-tidying-up-05.point: Kondo argues that tidying is not just about the home but about putting your life in order. Deciding what to keep helps people clarify what they value and gain confidence in their decisions. Many clients report changes in careers, relationships and health after tidying. She also describes treating belongings with gratitude, influenced by Shinto traditions, as a way to appreciate what you have.

nonviolent-communication-09.cue: How can you use NVC on yourself?
nonviolent-communication-09.point: Replace harsh self-talk like "I'm so stupid" with curiosity about the unmet need behind your action and the need you wanted to serve. Also translate "I have to" into "I choose to, because I value..." Driving your kids to school becomes a choice made because you value time with them. Owning your choices turns obligations into actions connected to what you care about.

the-1-page-marketing-plan-03.cue: What is a unique selling proposition, and why does it matter?
the-1-page-marketing-plan-03.point: A USP answers why a prospect should buy from you rather than a competitor. Dib argues most businesses describe themselves with generic claims such as quality service, which differentiate nothing. A strong USP is specific and benefit focused, like Domino's early promise of pizza in 30 minutes or it's free. Without one, you are forced to compete on price, which is a race to the bottom for small firms.

radical-candor-07.cue: What is the Get Stuff Done wheel?
radical-candor-07.point: Scott's cycle for achieving results collaboratively instead of by decree. Listen to ideas from the team, then clarify them so they are easy to evaluate. Debate the ideas openly, then decide, ideally pushing the decision to the people closest to the facts. Persuade the people who must implement it, execute, and then learn from the results so the next round of listening starts smarter.

act-like-a-lady-think-like-a-man-05.cue: What does Harvey say about standards in relationships?
act-like-a-lady-think-like-a-man-05.point: He argues that many women don't clearly state their standards, so men treat them according to the lowest acceptable behavior. Women should know what they want and require it from the start, whether that's respect, commitment or regular communication. Harvey says men will rise to meet clear expectations if they are interested. His broader message is to know your worth and not settle.

the-compound-effect-08.cue: What three outside influences shape your choices?
the-compound-effect-08.point: Input: what you feed your mind through news, shows and conversations shapes your thinking, so guard it carefully and add positive, growth-oriented content. Associations: you absorb the habits of the people around you, so spend more time with people who already have the traits you want. Environment: cluttered or limiting surroundings hold you back, so organize your space and change settings that keep you stuck.

to-sell-is-human-05.cue: What does Pink say about interrogative self talk?
to-sell-is-human-05.point: Before a pitch or challenge, Pink suggests asking yourself "Can I do this?" rather than declaring "I can do this!" Research by Ibrahim Senay found that people who asked themselves questions performed better on tasks than those who made affirmations. Questions prompt you to think about how you'll succeed, preparing strategies and building intrinsic motivation. This approach supports buoyancy.

the-seven-spiritual-laws-of-success-05.cue: What is the law of dharma?
the-seven-spiritual-laws-of-success-05.point: The law of dharma, or purpose in life, says everyone has a unique talent and a unique way of expressing it. Chopra suggests discovering your higher self, expressing your unique talents and serving humanity. When we combine our talent with service to others, we experience abundance and fulfillment. He suggests asking how you can help rather than what's in it for you.

white-fragility-03.cue: Why does DiAngelo argue white people struggle to see themselves racially?
white-fragility-03.point: She argues that white people in Western societies are often taught to see themselves as individuals rather than as members of a racial group, and to see whiteness as normal or neutral. This makes it hard to recognize advantages tied to race, such as being seen as the default. Segregated lives and limited cross racial relationships reinforce this. She calls for acknowledging racial identity as a step toward understanding inequality.

girl-stop-apologizing-02.cue: Which excuses does Hollis say hold women back?
girl-stop-apologizing-02.point: That a good woman puts herself last, when in fact being fulfilled makes you better for the people you love. That you're not capable, when everyone is bad at something new and success requires being willing to be bad for a while. That you have no time, when you must make time by replacing other activities. And that you can't have it all, when the goal is to feel centered, not perfectly balanced.

the-willpower-instinct-05.cue: How does dopamine affect self control?
the-willpower-instinct-05.point: Dopamine creates the promise of reward, driving us to seek things like food, shopping and notifications. But the anticipation is often more pleasurable than the actual reward. Marketers exploit this. McGonigal suggests noticing when dopamine drives you, testing whether rewards deliver, and harnessing dopamine for good habits by linking them to things you enjoy. Recognizing the promise of reward helps resist temptations.

first-break-all-the-rules-03.cue: Why do great managers select for talent?
first-break-all-the-rules-03.point: Buckingham and Coffman define talent as a recurring pattern of thought, feeling or behavior that can be productively applied. Skills and knowledge can be taught, but talents are largely fixed by adulthood. Great managers select people for talent rather than experience or intelligence alone, since talent determines performance. They look for striving, thinking and relating talents that fit the role.

business-model-generation-03.cue: What business model patterns does the book describe?
business-model-generation-03.point: The authors describe patterns including unbundling, separating customer relationship, product innovation and infrastructure businesses; the long tail, selling many niche products; multisided platforms, connecting distinct customer groups like Google connecting searchers and advertisers; free, where one segment is subsidized by another; and open business models, collaborating with outside partners. Recognizing patterns helps teams generate new ideas.

thinking-in-systems-08.cue: What other common system traps should you recognize?
thinking-in-systems-08.point: Policy resistance: actors with different goals pull against a policy until it accomplishes little, as with the war on drugs. Success to the successful: winners gain resources that help them win more, leading to monopolies. Drift to low performance: standards are set by recent performance, so each slightly worse year becomes the new normal. Recognizing the trap's structure points to the fix.

you-are-a-badass-03.also: The Gifts of Imperfection; Daring Greatly
you-are-a-badass-03.cue: Why does Sincero say you must love yourself before your life changes?
you-are-a-badass-03.point: Self loathing keeps people stuck because they do not believe they deserve better. Sincero urges readers to accept their quirks and flaws, stop comparing themselves to others, and treat themselves with the kindness they would give a friend. When you value yourself, you make braver choices and stop seeking approval. She suggests practical habits such as listing what you like about yourself and catching negative self talk before it spirals.

the-ideal-team-player-01.also: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team; Emotional Intelligence
the-ideal-team-player-01.cue: What are the three virtues of an ideal team player?
the-ideal-team-player-01.point: Patrick Lencioni, author of The Five Dysfunctions of a Team, argues ideal team players are humble, hungry and smart. Humble people lack excessive ego, share credit and put the team first. Hungry people are self motivated and diligent, always looking for more to do. Smart refers to people smarts: emotional intelligence, knowing how to interact well with others. Ideal team players possess all three.

deep-work-03.cue: What are Newport's four ways to schedule deep work?
deep-work-03.point: Seclusion removes almost all shallow work, like an author who is reachable only through an editor. Periodic scheduling sets aside whole days or weeks for depth. Daily scheduling reserves the same block each day, for example 8 to 11 a.m., which builds the strongest habit for most people. Ad hoc scheduling grabs deep work whenever a gap appears, which is flexible but hardest to sustain.

designing-your-life-08.cue: How do you prototype a life path before committing?
designing-your-life-08.point: Test ideas cheaply before investing years. Prototype conversations, which are informational interviews, let you hear what a career is really like from someone living it. Prototype experiences, like shadowing someone for a day, volunteering or a short project, give hands-on knowledge. These small tests help you fail fast and fail forward. They also give you access to the hidden job market, since most jobs are never advertised.

limitless-04.also: Moonwalking with Einstein; How to Read a Book
limitless-04.cue: What techniques does Kwik recommend for memory and speed reading?
limitless-04.point: For memory, he teaches mnemonic methods such as the memory palace, associating information with locations in a familiar place, and creating vivid, exaggerated images. For reading, he suggests using a finger or pointer as a visual guide and reducing subvocalization to increase speed. Researchers caution that speed reading often reduces comprehension, while memory techniques like the memory palace are well supported.

how-to-read-a-book-06.also: How to Read Literature Like a Professor
how-to-read-a-book-06.cue: How should you read different kinds of books?
how-to-read-a-book-06.point: Adler advises adjusting your approach to the genre. Practical books, such as self help, should be judged by whether their goals are worth pursuing and their means effective. Imaginative literature should be experienced rather than critiqued for arguments, by asking whether it is convincing and beautiful. History requires reading more than one account. Science and mathematics demand patience with technical terms, while philosophy requires asking what questions the author is trying to answer.

extreme-ownership-04.also: The One Thing; The Checklist Manifesto
extreme-ownership-04.cue: Why must leaders keep things simple and prioritize?
extreme-ownership-04.point: Complex plans fail under stress because people misunderstand them. Willink and Babin advise simple, clear and concise plans and orders. When multiple problems arise, leaders should prioritize and execute: relax, look around, make a call, determine the highest priority problem, apply resources to it, and then move to the next. Trying to solve everything at once leads to failure.

what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-02.cue: What are the habits that flaunt superiority?
what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-02.point: Winning too much, even over trivial arguments. Adding too much value by improving every idea, which takes ownership away from the person who had it. Passing judgment on others' ideas, even positively. Starting sentences with "no," "but" or "however," which says "you're wrong." Telling the world how smart you are. The fix for most of these is to simply say thank you and move on.

atomic-habits-07.cue: How can you make a habit you don't enjoy more attractive?
atomic-habits-07.point: We act because we anticipate a reward, and dopamine rises in that moment of wanting. So pair the habit with something you crave: "After dinner I study for an hour. After studying, I get to play video games." Clear also suggests reframing obligations as opportunities. Saying "I get to study" instead of "I have to study" points your attention at the reward and makes the effort easier to start.

thinking-in-systems-01.point: Donella Meadows defines a system as a set of elements interconnected in a way that achieves a purpose. A football team has players, rules and coaches working toward winning. The elements are easiest to see, but the interconnections and purpose shape behavior far more. Swap every player and the team still behaves like a team; change its purpose and everything changes.

21-lessons-for-the-21st-century-04.cue: Why does Harari argue that global problems need global cooperation?
21-lessons-for-the-21st-century-04.point: Humanity now forms one global civilization that shares economic systems, science and medicine, even while differing in religion and national identity. The three biggest threats, nuclear war, ecological collapse and disruptive technology, cross every border. A single nation cannot halt climate change or regulate AI alone. Harari argues that nationalism can offer belonging but no solutions to these challenges.

the-absolutely-true-diary-of-a-part-time.cue: How does the novel address loss and alcoholism?
the-absolutely-true-diary-of-a-part-time.point: Arnold suffers a series of deaths in one year, including his grandmother, killed by a drunk driver, his father's best friend, and his sister, who dies in a fire after a party. Alcoholism affects his family and community, which the novel connects to poverty and despair on reservations. Arnold copes through drawing, humor and basketball, and he refuses to give up hope. The book was praised for its honesty and also faced censorship challenges.

the-art-of-learning-01.cue: Who is Josh Waitzkin, and what is the book about?
the-art-of-learning-01.point: Waitzkin became a chess prodigy as a child, made famous by the film Searching for Bobby Fischer, and later became a world champion in Tai Chi Push Hands. In The Art of Learning he extracts general principles of excellence that apply across fields. He argues that the learning process itself can be mastered, and that the mental skills he developed in chess transferred to martial arts and beyond.

the-paradox-of-choice-02.also: Algorithms to Live By; The Happiness Hypothesis
the-paradox-of-choice-02.cue: What is the difference between maximizers and satisficers?
the-paradox-of-choice-02.point: Maximizers seek the best possible option and need to examine every alternative. Satisficers look for an option that is good enough and stop searching once they find it. Schwartz cites research showing maximizers often achieve objectively better outcomes, such as higher salaries, but feel less satisfied, more regretful and more depressed. Satisficing, deliberately accepting good enough, leads to greater happiness for most decisions.

the-8th-habit-02.cue: How do you find your voice, according to Covey?
the-8th-habit-02.point: Voice lies at the intersection of talent, what you are good at; passion, what energizes you; need, what the world will pay for; and conscience, what you sense you should do. Covey argues we develop our voice through our four intelligences: physical, mental, emotional and spiritual. He also stresses that people are born with gifts like freedom to choose, natural principles and intelligences that they can develop.

never-eat-alone-02.cue: Why does Ferrazzi say don't keep score?
never-eat-alone-02.point: Ferrazzi argues relationships should be based on generosity: give before you ask, without expecting immediate return. Introduce people, share information and help others reach their goals. This builds trust and goodwill. He criticizes transactional networking, where people only reach out when they need something. Generous connectors become central to networks, attracting opportunities naturally. Ferrazzi notes that the best time to build a network is before you need it.

bad-blood-04.cue: Who were the whistleblowers in the Theranos story?
bad-blood-04.point: Employees including Tyler Shultz, grandson of board member George Shultz, and Erika Cheung raised concerns internally and then contacted regulators and Carreyrou. Theranos responded with intimidation, legal threats and surveillance. Tyler Shultz's relationship with his grandfather was damaged. Their courage, along with Carreyrou's reporting at the Wall Street Journal beginning in 2015, led to investigations that unraveled the company.

emotional-intelligence-01.cue: What is emotional intelligence, according to Goleman?
emotional-intelligence-01.point: Daniel Goleman, a psychologist and science journalist, popularized the idea that emotional intelligence can matter as much as IQ for success in life. Drawing on work by Peter Salovey and John Mayer, he describes five domains: knowing your emotions, managing them, motivating yourself, recognizing emotions in others, and handling relationships. Unlike IQ, he argues, these skills can be learned and improved throughout life.

leaders-eat-last-01.also: Start With Why; The Culture Code
leaders-eat-last-01.cue: What is the Circle of Safety?
leaders-eat-last-01.point: Simon Sinek argues that great leaders create a Circle of Safety, an environment where people feel protected from dangers inside the organization, such as politics or layoffs, so they can focus on external challenges. Inside the circle, people trust each other and cooperate. Sinek takes the title from the U.S. Marine Corps, where officers eat after their troops, symbolizing leaders putting their people first.

the-body-keeps-the-score-05.cue: How does early attachment shape later life?
the-body-keeps-the-score-05.point: Babies depend on caregivers, and how reliably those caregivers respond shapes a child's inner map of the world. Securely attached children grow resilient. Insecurely attached children adapt by appearing calm while stressed inside, or by becoming anxious and clingy. Disorganized attachment, where the caregiver is a source of fear, is the most damaging, leaving people unsure whom to trust. These maps can change later through trauma or healing experiences.

poor-charlie-s-almanack-04.cue: What is the psychology of human misjudgment?
poor-charlie-s-almanack-04.point: In a famous talk, Munger lists about 25 psychological tendencies that cause poor decisions, such as reward and punishment superresponse, liking and disliking tendencies, doubt avoidance, inconsistency avoidance, social proof and the lollapalooza effect, where several tendencies combine to produce extreme results. Understanding these biases helps you avoid manipulation and make better decisions in business and life.

as-a-man-thinketh-04.cue: Why does Allen emphasize purpose and serenity?
as-a-man-thinketh-04.point: Allen argues that people without a central purpose fall prey to worries and fears. Setting a purpose and pursuing it with focus builds strength of character, even through failures. He ends by praising serenity, the calm that comes from self control and understanding. A calm person is more trusted and effective. He calls serenity one of the final lessons of culture and the fruit of life.

ego-is-the-enemy-03.also: Good to Great; The Dichotomy of Leadership
ego-is-the-enemy-03.cue: How does ego hurt us when we succeed?
ego-is-the-enemy-03.point: Success breeds entitlement, control and paranoia. Holiday cites Howard Hughes, whose ego led to destructive decisions, and contrasts him with figures like George Marshall, who declined credit and stayed humble. He advises remaining a student, managing yourself, and remembering that success is often partly luck. Ego leads leaders to believe their own press, which blinds them to risks.

brain-rules-02.cue: Why does Medina say exercise boosts brain power?
brain-rules-02.point: Our ancestors walked many miles a day, and the brain evolved under conditions of constant movement. Medina cites studies showing aerobic exercise improves executive function, memory and problem solving, and reduces the risk of dementia. Exercise increases blood flow and stimulates proteins that help neurons grow. He suggests treadmill desks and active classrooms to align modern life with biology.

the-emperor-of-all-maladies-06.cue: What did genetics reveal about cancer?
the-emperor-of-all-maladies-06.point: Researchers discovered oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes, showing that cancer arises when mutations accumulate in genes controlling cell growth. This led to targeted therapies such as Herceptin for HER2 positive breast cancer and Gleevec for chronic myeloid leukemia, which dramatically improved survival. Mukherjee notes cancer evolves and develops resistance, so it may never be defeated entirely, but can be managed as a chronic disease.

the-bhagavad-gita-01.point: The Bhagavad Gita, meaning Song of God, is a 700 verse Hindu scripture within the epic Mahabharata, dated roughly between the fifth and second centuries BC. It is a dialogue on a battlefield between the warrior prince Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna, who reveals himself as an incarnation of God. Arjuna, facing relatives and teachers in the opposing army, is overwhelmed with doubt, and Krishna teaches him about duty and the nature of reality.

first-things-first-05.also: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People; The 8th Habit
first-things-first-05.cue: Why does Covey emphasize principles over techniques?
first-things-first-05.point: Techniques for managing time fail when they aren't connected to deeper principles. Covey argues that principles such as integrity, service and fairness are like natural laws: they govern outcomes regardless of whether we believe in them. Basing priorities on principles gives stability and peace. He calls the inner sense that guides us toward them conscience.

the-everything-store-02.also: Thinking in Bets; Designing Your Life
the-everything-store-02.cue: What is Bezos's regret minimization framework?
the-everything-store-02.point: When deciding whether to leave his job at the hedge fund D. E. Shaw to start Amazon, Bezos imagined himself at age 80 and asked which choice he would regret more. He concluded he wouldn't regret trying and failing, but would regret never trying to participate in the internet's growth. This framework helps people make big decisions by focusing on long term regret rather than short term risk.

think-like-a-rocket-scientist-04.cue: Why does reframing the problem matter more than the solution?
think-like-a-rocket-scientist-04.point: We tend to apply familiar solutions to familiar-looking problems, a trap called the Einstellung effect. When an earlier Mars lander failed, the team stopped asking how to improve landing legs and asked how to land safely on Mars, which led to giant airbags that bounced the rover onto the surface. Separate strategy from tactics, and look at objects for what they are, not just what they are normally used for.

how-not-to-die-07.cue: What is Dr. Greger's Daily Dozen?
how-not-to-die-07.point: A checklist of what to eat each day: three servings of beans, one of berries, three of other fruit, one of cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, two of greens, two of other vegetables, one tablespoon of ground flaxseed, one serving of nuts, some spices such as turmeric, three servings of whole grains, five beverages such as water or tea, and daily exercise.

the-tipping-point-04.cue: What is the power of context?
the-tipping-point-04.point: Gladwell argues that behavior is strongly influenced by environment. He cites the broken windows theory, which holds that small signs of disorder, like graffiti, encourage more serious crime, and describes how New York's subway cleanup coincided with crime declines. Critics argue other factors explain the decline. He also discusses the rule of 150, the idea that groups function best below about 150 people.

a-random-walk-down-wall-street-05.also: Thinking, Fast and Slow; The Psychology of Money
a-random-walk-down-wall-street-05.cue: How does behavioral finance fit with Malkiel's view?
a-random-walk-down-wall-street-05.point: Malkiel acknowledges behavioral finance research showing investors are overconfident, follow the herd, fear losses more than they value gains and chase past performance. These biases lead people to buy high and sell low. However, he argues that even if markets are not perfectly efficient, it remains very hard to exploit inefficiencies consistently. The behavioral insights strengthen the case for indexing.

battlefield-of-the-mind-04.also: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living; The Power of Now
battlefield-of-the-mind-04.cue: What does Meyer say about worry and doubt?
battlefield-of-the-mind-04.point: Meyer describes worry as meditating on problems and argues it accomplishes nothing while robbing peace. Doubt and unbelief, she says, prevent believers from receiving what God offers. She encourages trusting God and living in the present rather than anxiously predicting the future. Practical steps include casting your cares on God in prayer and replacing anxious thoughts with gratitude.

as-a-man-thinketh-05.also: The Magic of Thinking Big; Grit
as-a-man-thinketh-05.cue: What does Allen say about thought and achievement?
as-a-man-thinketh-05.point: Allen argues that all achievement, whether in business, intellect or spirit, is the result of definitely directed thought. A person who wants to accomplish little needs to sacrifice little, while one who wants great things must sacrifice much, including indulgent and lazy habits of mind. He describes the dreamers as the saviors of the world, since every great achievement began as a vision. Cherishing a vision and working steadily toward it, he says, eventually makes it real.

what-color-is-your-parachute-05.also: Designing Your Life; Never Eat Alone
what-color-is-your-parachute-05.cue: What does Bolles say about informational interviewing?
what-color-is-your-parachute-05.point: Bolles recommends informational interviews, or trying on jobs, where you talk with people doing work that interests you to learn what it is really like. These conversations, often over coffee, reveal whether the job fits and build contacts. They are not job requests. Many people discover options they hadn't considered. The approach reduces risk before making a career change.

the-road-to-character-03.also: Leaders Eat Last; The Cost of Discipleship
the-road-to-character-03.point: Brooks profiles people who built strong character through struggle, such as Frances Perkins, who devoted her life to labor reform after witnessing the Triangle Shirtwaist fire; Dwight Eisenhower, who learned self restraint; Dorothy Day, who served the poor; George Marshall, who embodied duty; and Augustine, who turned from ambition to faith. Each confronted their weaknesses and committed to something larger.

who-not-how-03.also: Good to Great; The Ideal Team Player
who-not-how-03.cue: How do you find the right whos?
who-not-how-03.point: The authors suggest clarifying your vision and goals, then describing the result you want in an impact filter, a document that explains the purpose, importance and success criteria of a project. Share it with potential whos so they understand and can take ownership. Look for people who are excited by the work. Pay them well and treat them as partners, not just employees.

the-go-giver-02.cue: What are the Law of Value and the Law of Compensation?
the-go-giver-02.point: The Law of Value says your true worth is determined by how much more you give in value than you take in payment. A restaurant owner gives customers far more than they expect, which brings loyal customers. The Law of Compensation says your income is determined by how many people you serve and how well you serve them. To earn more, increase the number of people you help.

brief-answers-to-the-big-questions-08.cue: Is there intelligent life elsewhere in the universe?
brief-answers-to-the-big-questions-08.point: Hawking dismissed UFO reports as hoaxes or misunderstandings, expecting real alien contact to be obvious to all. He offered three reasons we haven't met anyone. Civilizations may be too far apart. Simple life may be common, but intelligence may be rare or may tend to destroy itself through war. Or life may be so unlikely that it arose only once, here, and we notice it only because we exist to observe it.

blue-ocean-strategy-02.point: The cornerstone of blue ocean strategy: offering a leap in value for buyers while lowering costs for the company. Instead of choosing between differentiation and low cost, you pursue both by rethinking which features the industry takes for granted. Cirque du Soleil dropped expensive circus staples like animal acts and star performers and added theater elements like storylines and artistic music, creating a new kind of entertainment.

hyperfocus-07.cue: What is scatterfocus, and how does it help you rest and create?
hyperfocus-07.point: Scatterfocus is intentional mind-wandering. Do something simple and enjoyable, like walking, knitting or showering, and let your thoughts roam, keeping a notepad handy. It recharges the mental energy that focus drains, so take a break about every 90 minutes. It also lets the brain connect unrelated pieces of knowledge, producing creative insights you would miss while concentrating.

crucial-conversations-02.also: Getting to Yes; Six Thinking Hats
crucial-conversations-02.cue: What is the pool of shared meaning?
crucial-conversations-02.point: Each person brings opinions, feelings and experiences to a conversation. The pool of shared meaning is the collection of information everyone contributes. The bigger the pool, the better the decisions, because people have more information and are more committed to results they helped shape. Silence or aggression keeps meaning out of the pool. Dialogue fills it.

creativity-inc-01.also: The Culture Code; No Rules Rules
creativity-inc-01.point: Ed Catmull, cofounder of Pixar and president of Pixar and Disney Animation, describes how he built a culture that sustained creativity, producing hits like Toy Story and Finding Nemo. He argues that managers must protect new ideas, confront hidden problems, and create an environment where people feel free to speak candidly. The book draws on Pixar's successes and failures, and his work reviving Disney Animation.

the-confidence-code-03.point: The authors report research suggesting confidence is partly heritable, influenced by genes affecting serotonin, dopamine and oxytocin. However, they emphasize that brains are plastic and that confidence can be built through experience. Taking risks, mastering skills and persisting through failure all strengthen confidence. Even people with genetic tendencies toward anxiety can become more confident.

trillion-dollar-coach-05.also: Leaders Eat Last; The Culture Code
trillion-dollar-coach-05.cue: What does Campbell's approach teach about leadership culture?
trillion-dollar-coach-05.point: Campbell argued that companies succeed through people, and that leaders should create environments where people can do their best work. He emphasized decision making with input from all perspectives, then getting the decision maker to decide. He championed courage, taking bold risks, and community, building connections beyond work. His principles show that coaching and caring are core leadership skills.

the-undercover-economist-04.point: Markets can fail when there are externalities, costs or benefits not reflected in prices, like pollution or traffic congestion; when information is unequal, as in the market for used cars, which George Akerlof called a market for lemons; and when there is market power. Harford argues smart policies, like congestion charges in London, can correct failures by making people pay for the costs they impose.

the-charisma-myth-01.also: How to Talk to Anyone; How to Win Friends and Influence People
the-charisma-myth-01.cue: Is charisma innate, according to Olivia Fox Cabane?
the-charisma-myth-01.point: Cabane argues that charisma is a set of learnable behaviors rather than an inborn trait. Experiments show charisma levels can be raised through practice, and charismatic people vary their charisma depending on the situation. She cites Marilyn Monroe walking unnoticed through a subway, then switching on her presence and being mobbed. Charisma comes from specific behaviors that make others feel good about themselves.

ikigai-05.also: The Happiness Project; Think Like a Monk
ikigai-05.cue: What are the ten rules of ikigai?
ikigai-05.point: The authors summarize ten rules: stay active and don't retire; take it slow; don't fill your stomach; surround yourself with good friends; get in shape for your next birthday; smile; reconnect with nature; give thanks; live in the moment; and follow your ikigai. Many Western interpretations combine ikigai with a Venn diagram of passion, mission, vocation and profession, which differs from its traditional Japanese meaning.

first-break-all-the-rules-04.also: Turn the Ship Around!; No Rules Rules
first-break-all-the-rules-04.cue: What does it mean to define the right outcomes?
first-break-all-the-rules-04.point: Great managers don't try to control how people do their work. They define the desired outcomes clearly and let each person find their own route. This respects individuality and encourages ownership. However, where accuracy or safety is critical, such as in compliance, managers do specify steps. Focusing on outcomes rather than methods prevents micromanagement.

the-ultimate-sales-machine-01.also: The One Thing; The 4 Disciplines of Execution
the-ultimate-sales-machine-01.cue: What is Chet Holmes's main idea in The Ultimate Sales Machine?
the-ultimate-sales-machine-01.point: Holmes, a sales and marketing trainer, argues that companies grow not by doing 4,000 things but by doing twelve things 4,000 times. He calls this pigheaded discipline and determination: choosing a few key strategies and practicing them relentlessly until they are mastered. Most businesses lack focus and constantly chase new ideas. His twelve strategies cover time management, training, marketing and sales.

the-magic-of-thinking-big-01.also: As a Man Thinketh; Awaken the Giant Within
the-magic-of-thinking-big-01.cue: What is the central idea of The Magic of Thinking Big?
the-magic-of-thinking-big-01.point: David Schwartz, a business professor, argues in this 1959 book that success is determined not by intelligence or background, but by the size of your thinking. People who believe big achieve big. Belief triggers the power to do, finding ways and means. He offers practical techniques for building confidence, setting goals and overcoming fear, illustrated with examples of salespeople and executives.

talk-like-ted-01.also: TED Talks: The Official TED Guide to Public Speaking; Made to Stick
talk-like-ted-01.cue: What is Talk Like TED about?
talk-like-ted-01.point: Communication coach Carmine Gallo analyzed hundreds of TED talks and interviewed speakers and researchers to identify what makes presentations persuasive. He distills nine secrets grouped under three themes: emotional, novel and memorable. Great presentations touch hearts, teach something new and are delivered in ways people remember. Gallo argues anyone can learn to present like the best TED speakers through preparation.

sell-or-be-sold-02.cue: Why does Cardone say commitment is the key to selling?
sell-or-be-sold-02.point: Cardone argues that salespeople must be totally committed to their product, company and customer. Belief in your product makes you persuasive. Without commitment, salespeople give up at the first objection. He compares commitment to marriage: you don't get to choose when to be committed. Committed salespeople persist through rejection and keep following up. He says salespeople who doubt their own product signal that doubt to customers.

the-shock-doctrine-01.point: Journalist Naomi Klein argues that governments and corporations have used crises such as wars, coups and natural disasters to push through free market policies, like privatization, deregulation and cuts to social spending, that the public would otherwise resist. She calls this disaster capitalism. She traces the idea to economist Milton Friedman's view that only a crisis produces real change. Critics, including many economists, dispute her portrayal of Friedman and causal claims.

digital-minimalism-03.cue: What are the three principles of digital minimalism?
digital-minimalism-03.point: Clutter is costly: many small apps and services each take a little time and attention, and together they drain more than they give. Optimization matters: decide which features of a tool actually serve your values and use only those. Intentionality is satisfying: choosing how you engage with technology, instead of reacting to it, feels rewarding in itself.

the-e-myth-revisited-01.point: Michael Gerber argues that most small businesses fail because of the entrepreneurial myth: the belief that businesses are started by entrepreneurs, when most are started by technicians, people skilled at a craft, like baking or plumbing, who suffer an entrepreneurial seizure. They assume that understanding the technical work means understanding how to run a business. Soon they are overwhelmed doing everything themselves.

the-compound-effect-07.cue: What is "Big Mo," and how do you build it?
the-compound-effect-07.point: Hardy's name for momentum. Getting started takes great effort, like pushing a stalled car, but once good choices become habits and habits become routines, progress accelerates and feels almost effortless. Build strong morning and evening routines, keep a steady rhythm and protect consistency above all. Doing too much too soon or breaking the rhythm kills momentum, and restarting takes far more energy than continuing.

surrounded-by-idiots-03.also: Quiet: The Power of Introverts; Crucial Conversations
surrounded-by-idiots-03.cue: What are Green and Blue behaviors?
surrounded-by-idiots-03.point: Greens are stable, patient and supportive. They value harmony and relationships, are good listeners and dislike sudden change and conflict, so they need reassurance and time to adjust. Blues are analytical, precise and cautious. They value facts, quality and detail, and can seem critical or slow to decide. With Blues, provide data, be thorough and give them time to analyze before asking for a decision.

the-5-levels-of-leadership-05.also: Good to Great; The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership
the-5-levels-of-leadership-05.point: Level 5 leaders develop other leaders to level 4, creating a legacy that outlasts them. Their reputation extends beyond their organization, and they create opportunities others cannot. Maxwell says few people reach this level, which requires years of growth and consistent character. Pinnacle leaders must stay humble, keep their inner circle honest, and plan for succession.

the-hacker-s-diet-03.cue: How should you plan calorie intake according to Walker?
the-hacker-s-diet-03.point: Walker suggests first measuring your current intake and trend, then cutting calories by a set amount, typically 500 to 1,000 per day, to lose one to two pounds a week. He recommends simple, consistent meals that are easy to count. Once you reach your goal, adjust intake to maintain the trend line at zero. He calls this a feedback control system: when the trend drifts up, eat a bit less.

never-eat-alone-04.cue: What does Ferrazzi say about following up and pinging?
never-eat-alone-04.point: Most people fail to follow up after meeting someone. Ferrazzi recommends following up within a day, referencing your conversation, and keeping in touch through regular pinging: brief messages like birthday wishes or articles of interest. Staying in touch consistently keeps relationships alive. He suggests dividing your network into tiers and contacting closer connections more often.

the-power-of-habit-06.cue: How do companies use habits to predict customer behavior?
the-power-of-habit-06.point: Duhigg describes Target analyzing purchase patterns to identify pregnant customers and send baby product coupons, since major life events are when shopping habits change. To avoid unsettling customers, Target mixed baby offers among unrelated ones so they felt familiar. Similarly, the song "Hey Ya!" became a hit only after radio stations sandwiched it between familiar songs. New things are most easily adopted when dressed in something old.

the-untethered-soul-01.also: The Power of Now; A New Earth
the-untethered-soul-01.cue: What is the main idea of The Untethered Soul?
the-untethered-soul-01.point: Michael Singer, a spiritual teacher and founder of a software company, argues that you are not your thoughts or emotions but the conscious awareness that observes them. Most people identify with the voice in their head, which causes suffering. By stepping back and watching thoughts and feelings without getting caught up in them, you can find inner peace and freedom. The book became a bestseller.

buy-rehab-rent-refinance-repeat-01.point: David Greene describes a real estate strategy: buy a property below market value, rehab it to increase its value, rent it to cover expenses, refinance based on the new higher value to pull your capital out, and repeat the process. The aim is to recycle the same capital into multiple properties, building a portfolio without needing new savings for each purchase. Success depends on buying well and controlling rehab costs.

traction-02.point: Wickman's Vision/Traction Organizer helps leadership teams answer eight questions: core values, core focus, ten year target, marketing strategy, three year picture, one year plan, quarterly priorities, called rocks, and issues. Getting everyone on the same page about where the company is going and how it will get there aligns the organization. The vision should be shared with all employees.

a-random-walk-down-wall-street-03.also: Business Adventures; Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital
a-random-walk-down-wall-street-03.cue: What does history teach about bubbles?
a-random-walk-down-wall-street-03.point: Malkiel describes speculative bubbles such as Dutch tulip mania in the 1630s, the South Sea Bubble, the Nifty Fifty stocks of the 1970s, the dot com bubble and the housing bubble. In each, investors abandoned valuation and bought because prices were rising. Bubbles show that markets can be irrational in the short term, but they eventually correct, often painfully.

radical-candor-06.cue: What are the three career conversations a manager should have with each person?
radical-candor-06.point: First, the life story: learn what has motivated the person over time by asking about their choices since childhood. Second, their dreams: ask what they want at the peak of their career and what skills would get them there. Third, an 18-month plan that links today's work to those dreams, listing what they need to learn and who could help them learn it.

why-we-sleep-03.cue: How does sleep change across a lifetime?
why-we-sleep-03.point: Before birth, fetuses spend up to 12 hours a day in REM, which wires the brain. In childhood, NREM sleep prunes and refines connections. Teenagers' clocks shift later, so early school start times clash with their biology. Deep sleep starts declining in your late twenties, and by 70 you may get about 90 percent less deep sleep than as a teenager, although older adults still need seven to nine hours.

the-happiness-project-04.also: The 5 Love Languages; The Happiness Hypothesis
the-happiness-project-04.cue: What did Rubin learn about relationships?
the-happiness-project-04.point: Rubin found that relationships are central to happiness. She resolved to stop nagging her husband, not expect praise, and show more appreciation. She noticed she was more irritable with those closest to her. For friendships, she resolved to remember birthdays, show up and be generous. She learned that acting the way she wanted to feel, being loving and cheerful, often created those feelings.

the-coaching-habit-01.cue: What is the main idea of The Coaching Habit?
the-coaching-habit-01.point: Michael Bungay Stanier argues managers should coach more by staying curious a little longer and rushing to give advice a little more slowly. Most managers default to advice, which keeps teams dependent and overloads the manager. Short coaching conversations built around seven questions can help people solve their own problems. Coaching should become a daily habit woven into ordinary interactions, not a formal event.

the-art-of-thinking-clearly-06.point: We judge the likelihood of events by how easily examples come to mind. Dramatic events like plane crashes feel more common than they are, while less memorable risks like diabetes are underestimated. Dobelli recommends seeking out base rates and statistics, and consulting people with different experiences, to avoid basing decisions on whatever is most vivid. Media coverage strongly shapes what is available in memory.

emotional-intelligence-2-0-02.also: Emotional Intelligence; Mindfulness in Plain English
emotional-intelligence-2-0-02.cue: How can you improve self awareness?
emotional-intelligence-2-0-02.point: Self awareness is the ability to accurately perceive your emotions as they happen and understand your tendencies across situations. Strategies include quitting the habit of treating feelings as good or bad, observing the ripple effects of your emotions on others, leaning into discomfort, recognizing physical signs of emotions, keeping a journal about emotions, and seeking feedback. Knowing what pushes your buttons helps you respond better.

the-hero-with-a-thousand-faces-01.point: Joseph Campbell, a scholar of comparative mythology, argued in 1949 that myths across cultures share a common structure he called the monomyth, or hero's journey. A hero ventures from the ordinary world into a region of supernatural wonder, encounters fabulous forces and wins a decisive victory, then returns with the power to bestow gifts on others. Campbell drew on psychology, especially Freud and Jung, to argue the pattern reflects universal human experience.

the-righteous-mind-06.cue: Why does Haidt say humans are 90 percent chimp and 10 percent bee?
the-righteous-mind-06.point: We are mostly selfish like chimpanzees, yet evolution also made us groupish like bees, able to work for the hive. Groups whose members cooperated outcompeted groups of selfish individuals. A hive switch lets us lose ourselves in something larger, through collective rituals, team spirit, synchronized movement or awe in nature. Wise leaders and organizations activate this switch to build trust and shared purpose.

biased-03.also: The New Jim Crow; Talking to Strangers
biased-03.cue: How does implicit bias play out in policing?
biased-03.point: Eberhardt analyzed data from Oakland police stops and found that officers stopped, searched and handcuffed Black residents more often, even after accounting for crime rates. Officers spoke less respectfully to Black drivers, as shown in body camera transcripts. She worked with departments to change policies. For example, requiring officers to ask whether a stop was intelligence led reduced stops of Black residents without increasing crime.

the-white-man-s-burden-04.cue: What does Easterly say about Western intervention?
the-white-man-s-burden-04.point: Easterly argues that Western efforts to impose institutions, economic reforms and political systems on poor countries, including structural adjustment programs by the IMF and World Bank and military interventions, have often failed. Institutions must emerge from local societies. Outsiders lack knowledge and legitimacy. He compares these efforts to colonialism, arguing they repeat its arrogance.

learning-how-to-learn-02.cue: Why is active recall better than rereading?
learning-how-to-learn-02.point: Pulling information out of memory, by reciting facts, writing them from memory or working a problem yourself, grows new connections between neurons and strengthens learning. Rereading notes or watching someone else solve a problem feels productive but builds little. Oakley and Sejnowski call active recall the single most effective study method. After reading a chapter, close the book and write down everything you can remember.

good-to-great-05.point: Like a hedgehog that knows one big thing, great companies focus on the intersection of three circles: what they can be the best in the world at, what drives their economic engine, measured by a single key denominator such as profit per customer, and what they are deeply passionate about. Walgreens focused on convenient drugstores. Clarity on this concept guided decisions for years.

the-hero-with-a-thousand-faces-05.also: Building a StoryBrand; Made to Stick
the-hero-with-a-thousand-faces-05.cue: How has Campbell's monomyth influenced modern storytelling?
the-hero-with-a-thousand-faces-05.point: George Lucas credited Campbell as a major influence on Star Wars, and Hollywood story consultant Christopher Vogler adapted the monomyth into a widely used guide for screenwriters. Many novels, films and video games follow its structure. Marketers and leaders also use the hero's journey to frame stories, often casting the customer or audience as the hero. Critics argue Campbell overgeneralized, smoothing over real differences between cultures' myths.

the-10x-rule-01.also: Sell or Be Sold; Can't Hurt Me
the-10x-rule-01.point: Grant Cardone argues that people consistently underestimate the effort needed to reach their goals. The 10X Rule says to set targets ten times higher than you think you want and then take ten times more action than you think necessary. Even if you fall short, you will achieve far more than with modest goals. Underestimating effort leads to disappointment and quitting when progress is slower than expected.

the-4-disciplines-of-execution-05.cue: What happens in a WIG session?
the-4-disciplines-of-execution-05.point: Discipline 4 creates a cadence of accountability through a weekly WIG session of twenty to thirty minutes. Each member reports on commitments made last week, reviews the scoreboard, and makes one or two new commitments that will move the lead measures. The meeting stays focused on the goal and excludes whirlwind issues. Because people make commitments to their peers rather than receiving orders, accountability becomes personal and progress becomes steady.

antifragile-08.cue: Why does Taleb insist on skin in the game?
antifragile-08.point: Fragility spreads when people gain the upside of risky decisions while others bear the downside, like bankers paid bonuses for profits but bailed out for losses. Taleb argues that anyone who makes decisions or predictions affecting others should share the consequences. An ancient rule required builders to face punishment if a house they built collapsed and killed its owner. Ask what an advisor would do in your position.

homo-deus-05.cue: Why does modern science threaten liberalism?
homo-deus-05.point: Liberalism rests on two beliefs: free will and an authentic inner self whose choices deserve respect. Neuroscience suggests decisions arise from biochemical processes that are either determined or random, never truly free. Research also shows we have an experiencing self that lives moment to moment and a narrating self that tells stories afterward, and they often disagree. If there is no single authentic voice, it is unclear whose choices liberalism protects.

no-drama-discipline-01.cue: What does No-Drama Discipline teach about the purpose of discipline?
no-drama-discipline-01.point: Neuropsychiatrist Daniel Siegel and parenting expert Tina Payne Bryson argue that discipline means teaching, not punishing. Its two goals are short term cooperation and long term development of the child's brain, helping children build self control, empathy and good judgment. Punishment may stop behavior temporarily but doesn't teach skills. Effective discipline builds connections in the developing brain.

the-laws-of-human-nature-01.also: The Art of War; Thinking, Fast and Slow
the-laws-of-human-nature-01.cue: What is The Laws of Human Nature about?
the-laws-of-human-nature-01.point: Robert Greene, author of The 48 Laws of Power, presents eighteen laws describing the hidden forces that drive human behavior, drawing on psychology and stories of historical figures. He argues that understanding these laws helps us become calmer, more strategic observers of people, and less ruled by our own emotions. Each law describes a tendency, such as irrationality, narcissism or envy, and how to manage it in ourselves and others.

who-will-cry-when-you-die-04.also: The Five People You Meet in Heaven; Give and Take
who-will-cry-when-you-die-04.cue: What does Sharma say about relationships and kindness?
who-will-cry-when-you-die-04.point: Sharma emphasizes that relationships matter most at the end of life. He suggests spending time with loved ones, practicing random acts of kindness, writing thank you notes and listening deeply. He encourages forgiving others, since holding grudges harms the one holding them. Treating everyone with respect and being generous creates a life that others will remember warmly.

strangers-in-their-own-land-04.also: The Righteous Mind; How Democracies Die
strangers-in-their-own-land-04.cue: How does Hochschild describe the role of emotion in politics?
strangers-in-their-own-land-04.point: Hochschild argues that political beliefs are rooted in emotions, such as pride, loss and resentment, and shaped by identity. Her subjects took pride in endurance, religion and self reliance, and felt that their values were mocked. She argues that understanding these feelings, not just arguments, is necessary to bridge divides. She describes how Donald Trump's candidacy appealed to these emotions.

technological-revolutions-and-financial-.cue: What are the two periods of each surge?
technological-revolutions-and-financial-.point: Perez divides each surge into an installation period and a deployment period. During installation, financial capital funds the new technology, leading to rapid innovation, speculation and a financial bubble. A crash follows, creating a turning point. During deployment, the technology spreads throughout the economy, production capital takes the lead, and growth becomes broader and more stable. Institutions adapt to the new paradigm.

economics-in-one-lesson-04.cue: What does Hazlitt argue about tariffs and protectionism?
economics-in-one-lesson-04.point: Tariffs protect certain domestic industries, saving visible jobs. But consumers pay higher prices, leaving less money to spend on other goods, and foreign countries have fewer dollars to buy exports. The jobs lost in other industries are invisible. Hazlitt argues free trade allows each country to specialize in what it does best, increasing total wealth. Protectionism benefits a few at the expense of many.

the-emperor-of-all-maladies-04.also: Brief Answers to the Big Questions
the-emperor-of-all-maladies-04.cue: What was the War on Cancer?
the-emperor-of-all-maladies-04.point: In 1971 President Nixon signed the National Cancer Act, backed by advocates like Mary Lasker and Farber, who argued that money and focus could cure cancer, as the Manhattan Project produced the atomic bomb. Funding increased dramatically, but cures proved elusive because researchers did not yet understand cancer's biology. Mukherjee argues the campaign overpromised, though it built infrastructure that later enabled breakthroughs.

the-7-habits-of-highly-effective-people-.cue: What is the time management matrix (Habit 3)?
the-7-habits-of-highly-effective-people-.point: Tasks are sorted by urgency and importance. Quadrant 1 holds urgent and important crises. Quadrant 2 holds important but not urgent work like exercise, planning and building relationships. Quadrant 3 holds urgent but unimportant interruptions, usually other people's priorities. Quadrant 4 holds neither, like mindless scrolling. Effective people spend most of their time in Quadrant 2, which prevents many Quadrant 1 crises from arising.

the-inner-game-of-tennis-03.also: Mindfulness in Plain English; Radical Acceptance
the-inner-game-of-tennis-03.cue: Why does Gallwey say to let go of judgments?
the-inner-game-of-tennis-03.point: When Self 1 labels a shot as good or bad, it triggers emotional reactions and tightens the body, which leads to more errors. Gallwey suggests observing what happens without judgment, such as noticing the ball landed a foot long, and letting Self 2 adjust automatically. Nonjudgmental awareness provides accurate feedback, while judgment creates anxiety. Natural learning works through observation, not criticism.

give-and-take-04.also: To Sell Is Human; The Coaching Habit
give-and-take-04.cue: How do givers communicate and influence?
give-and-take-04.point: Grant argues givers use powerless communication: asking questions, seeking advice, expressing vulnerability and talking tentatively. These approaches build trust and influence more effectively than dominant styles. Seeking advice makes others invested in your success. Givers also recognize others' potential and invest in developing them, often helping them achieve more than expected. Grant notes that this style works especially well for givers, who are comfortable sharing credit.

girl-wash-your-face-04.cue: What should you do when someone tells you no?
girl-wash-your-face-04.point: Rejection doesn't mean stop; it means find another route. Hollis had many doors closed in her career and treated each "no" as a reason to change course rather than give up. She also argues that daydreaming isn't a waste of time. Visualizing your goals in vivid detail clarifies what you want and keeps you motivated to pursue it.

the-challenger-sale-05.also: Never Split the Difference; Pitch Anything
the-challenger-sale-05.cue: What does taking control mean for a Challenger?
the-challenger-sale-05.point: Taking control means being assertive, not aggressive, about the sale's direction and money. Challengers push back when customers make unreasonable demands, steer conversations toward value instead of discounts, and keep the deal moving. They are comfortable with tension and do not give in to every request. The authors argue that many reps cave too quickly, while controlled assertiveness builds respect and leads to better outcomes.

multipliers-01.also: The Coaching Habit; Turn the Ship Around!
multipliers-01.point: Liz Wiseman, a former Oracle executive, identifies two kinds of leaders. Multipliers use their intelligence to amplify the smarts and capabilities of those around them, getting much more from their teams. Diminishers drain intelligence and energy, believing they need to be the smartest person in the room. Her research suggests Multipliers get about twice as much from people as Diminishers do.

how-not-to-die-02.cue: Why does Greger recommend a whole-food, plant-based diet?
how-not-to-die-02.point: He argues that diets heavy in meat, dairy, eggs and processed food drive heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure and many cancers, while whole plant foods help prevent them. He cites studies in which vegetarians who returned to eating meat saw their risk of disease rise sharply and their life expectancy fall. Large population studies link plant-heavy diets to lower mortality even after controlling for weight and wealth.

the-charisma-myth-02.cue: What are the three core elements of charisma?
the-charisma-myth-02.point: Cabane names presence, power and warmth. Presence means being fully attentive in the moment, so people feel heard. Power means being perceived as able to affect the world, through influence, intelligence, wealth or status. Warmth means goodwill toward others, the sense that you would use your power to help them. Different combinations create different charisma styles, such as focus, visionary, kindness and authority charisma.

thinking-in-systems-03.cue: Why do we misjudge how to change a stock?
thinking-in-systems-03.point: People focus on stocks more than flows, and on inflows more than outflows. When population rises, we think of births and forget that falling death rates also grow it. A company trying to grow headcount thinks about hiring and neglects reducing the number of people who quit. You can fill a tub by turning up the faucet or by plugging the drain, and the drain is often cheaper.

blue-ocean-strategy-05.cue: What is the four actions framework?
blue-ocean-strategy-05.point: Four questions for redrawing a value curve. Which factors the industry takes for granted should be eliminated? Which should be reduced well below the standard? Which should be raised well above it? Which should be created that the industry has never offered? Eliminating and reducing cuts costs, while raising and creating adds new value, which is how value innovation achieves both at once.

the-black-swan-01.cue: What makes an event a Black Swan?
the-black-swan-01.point: Three features. It is a rare outlier that nothing in the past pointed to convincingly. It has an extreme impact. And after it happens, people construct explanations that make it seem predictable all along. The name comes from Europeans who assumed all swans were white until they found black swans in Australia. The internet, 9/11 and the 2008 financial crisis are all Black Swans.

what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-01.cue: Why does Marshall Goldsmith say success can hold you back?
what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-01.point: Successful people believe their habits made them successful, including the bad ones. They succeed in spite of certain behaviors, not because of them. As people move up, technical skill matters less and interpersonal behavior matters more. Goldsmith, an executive coach, has found that small, repeated flaws like needing to win or failing to listen are often what stalls talented people from reaching the top.

moneyball-04.cue: What did Beane's own career teach him?
moneyball-04.point: Beane was a top prospect, praised by scouts for his physical tools, but failed as a major league player because he lacked the mental approach. This experience made him skeptical of scouting judgment. He learned that how players looked mattered less than how they performed. His story illustrates the gap between perceived potential and actual results.

the-righteous-mind-02.cue: Why does Haidt say we reason like politicians, not scientists?
the-righteous-mind-02.point: Moral reasoning evolved to protect our reputation and win allies more than to find truth. We care intensely about what others think of us, even when we deny it. An inner press secretary finds evidence for what we already believe; smarter people just generate more arguments for their own side. We ask "Can I believe it?" about ideas we like and "Must I believe it?" about ideas we dislike.

tiny-habits-01.also: Atomic Habits; The Power of Habit
tiny-habits-01.cue: What is the Tiny Habits method?
tiny-habits-01.point: BJ Fogg, a Stanford behavior scientist, argues that lasting change comes from starting very small, not relying on motivation. A tiny habit is a behavior you can do in under 30 seconds, such as flossing one tooth, anchored to an existing routine and followed by a moment of celebration. Small successes build confidence and naturally grow. Fogg says you change best by feeling good, not by feeling bad.

the-china-study-05.also: Merchants of Doubt; Fast Food Nation
the-china-study-05.cue: Why do the Campbells criticize the health system and industry?
the-china-study-05.point: They argue the food and pharmaceutical industries influence nutrition research and government guidelines, and that medicine focuses on drugs and surgery rather than diet. Researchers who challenge prevailing views face resistance, and the public receives confusing messages. The authors call for nutrition education in medical schools. Critics in turn accuse the book of selective use of evidence.

the-obstacle-is-the-way-01.cue: What is the main idea of The Obstacle Is the Way?
the-obstacle-is-the-way-01.point: Ryan Holiday draws on Stoic philosophy, especially Marcus Aurelius, to argue that obstacles are not barriers but opportunities. The impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way. He presents three disciplines for turning obstacles into advantages: perception, action and will. Examples range from John D. Rockefeller to Thomas Edison to Amelia Earhart.

measure-what-matters-02.also: The 4 Disciplines of Execution; Built to Last
measure-what-matters-02.cue: What are the four superpowers of OKRs?
measure-what-matters-02.point: Doerr describes four benefits. Focus and commit to priorities: choosing a few objectives clarifies what matters. Align and connect for teamwork: transparent OKRs show how each person's work connects to company goals. Track for accountability: regular check ins monitor progress. Stretch for amazing: ambitious goals push teams beyond comfort, where achieving 70 percent may count as success.

so-you-want-to-talk-about-race-05.point: Black students are suspended and expelled at far higher rates than white students for similar behavior, and teachers may perceive Black children as older, angrier or more threatening. Missing school leads to falling behind and dropping out, and a growing police presence in schools turns discipline into arrests. Students arrested at school are more likely to be arrested as adults, so early disparities can follow children for life.

12-rules-for-life-01.cue: What does Peterson mean by "Stand up straight with your shoulders back"?
12-rules-for-life-01.point: Peterson uses lobsters to argue that dominance hierarchies are ancient and that serotonin levels track status, influencing posture and confidence. A defeated lobster shrinks and its chemistry changes, making it more likely to lose again. Humans show similar feedback loops. Adopting an upright posture and voluntarily accepting life's challenges signals to yourself and others that you are prepared to engage. Some biologists dispute how far the lobster analogy applies to people.

the-selfish-gene-04.point: Dawkins coined the word meme to describe a unit of cultural transmission, such as a tune, catchphrase or idea, that spreads from mind to mind by imitation. Like genes, memes compete for survival, mutate and spread when they are good at being copied, regardless of whether they benefit their hosts. Religion, fashion and slogans can all be seen as memes. The concept became the basis of memetics.

the-communist-manifesto-01.cue: What is the central claim of The Communist Manifesto?
the-communist-manifesto-01.point: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, writing in 1848, open with the claim that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. Freeman and slave, lord and serf, and now bourgeoisie and proletariat stand in opposition. Under capitalism, society is splitting into two great classes: the owners of the means of production and the workers who sell their labor. They predict this conflict will lead to revolution.

the-chimp-paradox-02.cue: How should you manage your Chimp?
the-chimp-paradox-02.point: You cannot defeat the Chimp, but you can manage it. Peters suggests letting it exercise, by venting emotions in a safe space, then boxing it with facts and logic once it has calmed down. Rewarding it with bananas, such as treats for achieving goals, also helps. Learning to recognize when the Chimp has hijacked you is the first step. The aim is to work with your emotions rather than be controlled by them.

the-bhagavad-gita-02.cue: What does Krishna teach about duty, or dharma?
the-bhagavad-gita-02.point: Krishna tells Arjuna that he must fulfill his dharma, his duty as a warrior, even when it is painful. It is better to perform one's own duty imperfectly than another's perfectly. Avoiding action out of fear or attachment is not virtuous. This teaching has been interpreted in many ways, including as a call to responsibility in daily life, and figures like Gandhi read the battle metaphorically as an inner struggle.

learning-how-to-learn-01.cue: What are focused and diffuse modes of thinking?
learning-how-to-learn-01.point: Focused mode is concentrated attention on a specific problem, using neural pathways you have already built. It handles detail but can get stuck in familiar patterns. Diffuse mode is the relaxed, wandering state of a walk or shower, when the brain links distant ideas. Hard problems need both: focus until you get stuck, take a real break to let diffuse mode work, then return to focus to finish.

the-e-myth-revisited-03.also: The Checklist Manifesto; Fast Food Nation
the-e-myth-revisited-03.point: Gerber argues that the franchise prototype, pioneered by companies like McDonald's, provides a model for any business. The business itself becomes the product, a system that delivers consistent results regardless of who runs it. Every task is documented and systematized, so ordinary people can produce extraordinary results. Owners should build their business as if they were going to franchise it, even if they never do.

thinking-in-systems-05.cue: What is a reinforcing feedback loop?
thinking-in-systems-05.point: A loop that amplifies change, making a stock grow or shrink faster and faster. The more money in a savings account, the more interest it earns. The more people, the more births. It can also run downhill: eroded soil holds fewer roots, which leads to more erosion, and a shortage of toilet paper makes people buy more, deepening the shortage. Look for reinforcing loops behind exponential growth or collapse.

the-glass-castle-03.cue: How did Walls's parents both nurture and neglect their children?
the-glass-castle-03.point: Rex taught the children physics, geology and math, and Rose Mary encouraged reading and art. They valued independence and creativity. But they also left the children hungry, unsupervised and exposed to danger. Jeannette was badly burned at age three while cooking alone. Her parents rejected help and taught that hardship builds character. The memoir shows love and neglect existing side by side.

six-thinking-hats-03.also: Thinking in Bets; The Art of Thinking Clearly
six-thinking-hats-03.cue: What do the black and yellow hats represent?
six-thinking-hats-03.point: The black hat represents caution and critical judgment: identifying risks, weaknesses and reasons something might not work. It is valuable but can dominate thinking if overused. The yellow hat represents optimism: looking for benefits, value and reasons something will work. Using both deliberately ensures a balanced evaluation rather than reflexive criticism or uncritical enthusiasm.

built-to-last-05.also: The Culture Code; The Dichotomy of Leadership
built-to-last-05.cue: What are cult like cultures and the tyranny of the OR?
built-to-last-05.point: Visionary companies have intense, almost cult like cultures, with strong indoctrination and fit, so people either love working there or leave. They also reject the tyranny of the OR, the belief that you must choose between opposites like stability or change. Instead they embrace the genius of the AND, pursuing both continuity and change, purpose and profit, at the same time.

hyperfocus-01.cue: Why does Chris Bailey say attention matters more than time?
hyperfocus-01.point: Productivity experts usually focus on managing time, but Bailey argues that the quality of our attention determines the quality of our work and lives. He describes two modes: hyperfocus, deliberately concentrating on a single task to be productive, and scatterfocus, deliberately letting the mind wander to be creative and rest. Both require choosing where attention goes instead of running on autopilot.

battlefield-of-the-mind-05.cue: What kinds of minds does Meyer describe?
battlefield-of-the-mind-05.point: Meyer contrasts a normal mind, which she describes as being at rest and peaceful, with abnormal states. A wandering mind cannot concentrate. A confused mind tries to reason everything out. A doubtful mind questions God's promises. A judgmental mind criticizes others. A passive mind lets the enemy fill it with thoughts. She argues that each can be corrected through discipline, prayer and focus on Scripture.

rich-dad-s-cashflow-quadrant-02.also: The E-Myth Revisited; Who Not How
rich-dad-s-cashflow-quadrant-02.cue: Why does Kiyosaki favor the B and I quadrants?
rich-dad-s-cashflow-quadrant-02.point: Employees and self employed people depend on their own labor, so their income stops when they stop working. They also pay higher taxes on earned income. Business owners and investors generate passive income from systems and assets, enjoy tax advantages and can scale. Kiyosaki argues that schools train people to be employees rather than owners. Critics note his claims about taxes and investing are oversimplified.

make-it-stick-06.cue: What role does feedback play in learning, and when should it come?
make-it-stick-06.point: Corrective feedback stops you from locking in wrong answers. Slightly delayed feedback works better than instant correction, which can become a crutch, like training wheels you never learn to ride without. The best sequence is to test yourself first, then check your answers and spend your study time on the questions you got wrong.

no-rules-rules-01.cue: What is Netflix's culture of freedom and responsibility?
no-rules-rules-01.point: Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings and INSEAD professor Erin Meyer describe how Netflix built a culture with minimal rules, giving employees unusual freedom in exchange for high responsibility. Hastings learned from his first company, where rules and processes made it rigid and drove away talented people. At Netflix, he aimed to build talent density, candor and freedom step by step.

david-and-goliath-02.cue: What is the inverted U curve?
david-and-goliath-02.point: Many advantages help up to a point and then become harmful. Smaller class sizes improve learning, but very small classes lose the energy of discussion. Parents with some money raise children more easily, but great wealth can make it harder to teach the value of hard work. Gladwell argues people often assume more is always better, when in fact many resources follow an inverted U pattern.

essentialism-06.cue: What is a buffer, and why does McKeown recommend one?
essentialism-06.point: A buffer is extra time or resources set aside for the unexpected. People consistently underestimate how long tasks will take, a habit known as the planning fallacy. McKeown recommends adding about 50 percent to your time estimate for any important project. With a buffer, surprises become manageable instead of turning into crises that force you to drop priorities. Preparation for the worst case is a form of discipline rather than pessimism.

thinking-fast-and-slow-09.cue: What is the difference between the experiencing self and the remembering self?
thinking-fast-and-slow-09.point: The experiencing self lives moment to moment. The remembering self keeps score and makes future choices. Memory follows the peak-end rule, judging an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, and it ignores duration. That is why we pick holidays for the memories. Kahneman suggests giving the experiencing self more weight: shorten your commute and spend more time socializing and exercising.

superforecasting-02.point: Borrowing from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin, Tetlock describes hedgehogs as experts with one big idea who fit everything into it, often confidently and dramatically. Foxes know many little things, draw on diverse sources and adjust their views. Foxes made better forecasts than hedgehogs, though hedgehogs often got more media attention because their certainty made good television.

the-4-disciplines-of-execution-02.cue: What is Discipline 1, focus on the wildly important?
the-4-disciplines-of-execution-02.point: Choose one or at most two wildly important goals, or WIGs, instead of many priorities. The more goals a team pursues, the fewer it achieves with excellence. Each WIG should be stated as a measurable shift from X to Y by a deadline, such as raising customer satisfaction from 70 to 85 percent by December. Leaders must accept leaving good ideas undone so the team can make real progress on what matters most.

the-magic-of-thinking-big-02.point: Schwartz calls excuses the failure disease. Common forms include health excusitis, intelligence excusitis, age excusitis and luck excusitis. People with excusitis blame circumstances for their failures. He argues attitude matters more than intelligence, and that the right thinking turns perceived handicaps into motivation. To cure excusitis, refuse to talk about your problems and focus on what you can do.

imagined-communities-05.cue: How did census, map and museum shape colonial nations?
imagined-communities-05.point: In a later edition, Anderson describes how colonial states used the census to classify populations into categories, maps to define territories, and museums to present histories. These tools shaped how colonized people came to imagine their nations. When independence came, new nations often inherited these colonial boundaries and categories. Nationalism thus drew on tools of the very colonial powers it opposed.

the-untethered-soul-03.also: Radical Acceptance; The Gifts of Imperfection
the-untethered-soul-03.cue: What does Singer mean by opening the heart?
the-untethered-soul-03.point: Singer argues that when we feel pain, such as jealousy or insecurity, we tend to close our hearts to protect ourselves. These blocked energies, which he calls samskaras, stay inside and affect future reactions. Instead, he suggests relaxing and allowing feelings to pass through, keeping the heart open. Letting go of stored pain frees energy and allows joy to flow.

what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-06.cue: What other habits quietly damage leaders' reputations?
what-got-you-here-won-t-get-you-there-06.point: Withholding information, which breeds distrust even when it is unintentional. Claiming credit you don't deserve. Playing favorites, often by rewarding people who flatter you. And goal obsession, where focus on a target makes you ruthless toward people in your way. Each is fixable: share information routinely, credit others publicly and ask whether your methods are hurting people around you.

tools-of-titans-04.cue: What wisdom does Tools of Titans share about life?
tools-of-titans-04.point: Ferriss includes advice like practicing fear setting, writing down worst case scenarios to reduce anxiety.
